TPU vs GPU

This is not a tour of spec sheets.
Run one FlashAttention kernel on both chips; find the step where they diverge.

Two questions, one path. ① How do the two chips differ in hardware? ② Run one op end to end: where does each difference surface? The verdict: they differ everywhere, all because of one decision.

TPU side v7 (Ironwood) GPU side B200 teardown measured on GB300 NVL72 Sources public source code + own measurements ⏱ 109 min · 43 figures

Course author Chris Yang·Google Cloud AI Infra architect

This lecture has instructor notes.

They cover how to teach it: segment goals, pauses, common misconceptions, likely questions. The content is here.

Presenting: lines, figure cues and timing are written out. Self-study: give the script to an AI for a TA who knows the lecture and how to teach it.

⛔ Don't open before class: two warm-ups We do them together in class; peeking spoils them.

First, a question from last lecture

Last lecture we took apart DeepSeek V3: 671B total parameters, but each token activates only 37B—that’s MoE.
If only 37B are active, is it as cheap to serve as a 37B dense model?
What does MoE actually save?

It saves compute, not memory.
Each token takes only the 37B path, so the compute saving is real. But all 671B of weights stay resident, every byte: no one knows which experts the next token picks, so all sit in HBM. “37B active” ≠ “as cheap to serve as 37B.”

⭐ The idea behind the question: memory and compute are separate, and move independently. Last lecture kept the two accounts apart.
This lecture adds a third: bandwidth. What decides whether an op is fast is often neither of the first two. Section 1 works out the exchange rate between compute and data movement.

Two more numbers to guess (answers now, the “why” in Section 3)

We will take both chips apart, layer by layer. First, guess: how many pieces does each chip divide its compute into?
On B200 the unit is called a Tensor Core; on v7 it is the MXU. Both do matrix multiply-accumulate.
The question is the total per chip.

① How many Tensor Cores does a full B200 have?
② How many MXUs in a full TPU v7?

Answer the two independently; the answer appears once both are picked.

B200: 592. v7: 4.
592 = 148 SMs × 4 Tensor Cores per SM; 4 = 2 TensorCores × 2 MXUs per core. A 148× difference in count.

⭐ The surprise: The two chips differ by only 15% in MACs per cycle: 606,208 on B200 versus 524,288 on v7.
The same compute, cut into 592 small pieces vs. 4 large ones.

⭐ The “why” is an IOU. Keep the question in mind. How can the count differ by 148× while the total is nearly the same? What does each side pay for cutting fine vs. coarse? All of Section 3 answers these two. When you get there, you'll recognize which figure holds the answer.

Section 0

First, a premise: two chips, two origins

The figure below is the lecture's only premise. With it, you can predict each section's differences. Look, then move on: Section 1 is one division; Section 2 starts the teardown.

Think for thirty seconds first You must design a chip without knowing what customers will run. What do you do? Now flip it: you know from day one it runs just one kind of workload. The gap between the answers is the figure below.
Up front: we don't rank the chips Both origins were right at the time; each still carries its cost. You won't read “which is better,” only “who decides this, on this side.”
If you keep one sentence: they differ everywhere, all because of one decision. Section 2 names it.

Section 1

The dividing line: two chips, same appetite

This section computes one number: the compute-to-movement exchange rate, operations per byte moved. Every later op is checked against it: below the line, bandwidth rules; above it, compute. No conclusions here.

Think for thirty seconds first Only two spec-sheet numbers matter: operations per second and bytes moved per second.
How do you combine them into something useful? Hint: not “which is bigger,” but something that can judge a particular op.

1.1 ⭐ Compute ÷ bandwidth: both vendors, one number

Divide the two spec numbers: operations per second by bytes per second. The ratio is operations done in the time one byte moves. A floor: each byte moved needs this many operations just to feed compute.

Everyone asks: both sides have eight 24 GB HBM3E stacks; why different bandwidth?
“HBM3E” names the generation, not the speed grade. Each stack: 1,024 data lines; bandwidth = 1,024 × pin rate. HBM3E spans 8.0–⁠9.6 Gbps/pin. Backing out: v7 runs 7.2 Gbps (7.37 TB/s ÷ 8, exact, though 7.2 is outside 8.0–9.6), GB200 about 7.8.
The buyer picks the grade (power, cooling, reliability, supply); it isn't the chip's ceiling. (Why not top grade? That also exposes a hole in our own numbers.)

⭐ Same eight 24 GB HBM3E stacks: why 7.37 vs. 8.0? Pin-level math finds a hole in our own numbers

The HBM configuration is identical: eight HBM3E stacks, 24 GB each, 192 GB total. (The v7 “eight stacks” comes from Google Cloud's Ironwood technical blog; the B200 figure from NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture page.)

Then why does the bandwidth differ? Because “HBM3E” is not a speed; it is a range of speeds. Every stack has 1,024 data lines, and bandwidth = 1,024 × per-pin data rate. Pin rates from 8.0 to 9.6 Gbps all count as HBM3E (Micron lists a pin speed above 9.2 Gbps and more than 1.2 TB/s; Rambus lists 9.6 Gb/s and 1,229 GB/s). “Same HBM3E” does not mean “same bandwidth.”

Working backwards to each side's grade:

  • TPU v7: official 7.37 TB/s ÷ 8 stacks = 921.6 GB/s per stack → 1,024 bit × 7.2 Gbps ÷ 8 = 921.6. Exactly 7.2 Gbps (1,024 × 7.2 ÷ 8 = 921.6, × 8 stacks = 7,372.8 GB/s).
    ⚠️ But 7.2 falls outside the 8.0–9.6 range, as does GB200's 7.81: neither back-calculated rate is a nominal grade, so each official figure hides an unstated down-clock or accounting convention. Both sides get the same treatment.
  • GB200: official 8 TB/s ÷ 8 stacks = 1,000 GB/s per stack → back-calculated pin rate 7.81 Gbps. ⚠️ That isn't any nominal grade.
⛔ So the “0.13% relative difference” line is no longer a selling point That 7.81 means “8 TB/s” hides a convention NVIDIA never states, with two plausible readings:
•  Decimal: the vendor down-clocks and reports exactly 8,000 GB/s (down-clocking HBM is routine)
•  Binary: it is actually the 8.0 Gbps grade, 8 × 1,024 GB/s = 8,192 GB/s, rounded to “8” in public specs
The two readings differ by 2.4%. Work it out: 2,500 ÷ 8.000 = 312.5, whereas 2,500 ÷ 8.192 = 305.2.
The third digit of “312.9 vs. 312.5” falls entirely inside that 2.4%.

⭐ The conclusion stands; the precision doesn't: the two exchange rates really are in the same range (within a few percent), so the section's result holds. But “0.13% apart” is false precision; don't sell it.
⭐⭐ The most useful part: “is this number binary or decimal?” is one of Section 6's four questions. Here it lands on this lecture's own headline number. Aim those four questions at your own material first, not just at others'.
⭐ So why not run at the top grade? Four reasons, hard to soft In one line: HBM's philosophy is “wide, not fast”. 1,024 lines per stack, so no line must run fast. So data rate is a tunable knob, not a spec to max out.

① Power. I/O dynamic power tracks data rate, and higher rates often need more voltage. In a 700–800 W+ package, HBM is no rounding error: top-grade bandwidth is paid from the compute budget.
② Heat, the worst one for HBM. In a 3D stack the bottom die is farthest from the heat sink; its heat can't escape. And hot DRAM must refresh more often. Refresh costs power and takes bus time. Counterintuitively, a hot, throttling top grade may deliver less than a steady lower one.
③ ⭐ Reliability, which answers Section 0's “is simpler more robust?” According to hyperscaler data, HBM failure is the leading cause of GPU failures, more often than any other datacenter chip. (Cited by SemiAnalysis, no specific numbers given.) In a 9,000+-chip pod, per-chip failure rate × scale = training interruption rate. Dropping one speed grade to buy cluster-wide uptime is an easy trade.
④ Supply and system balance. Top bins are costly and scarce; sourcing hundreds of thousands reliably is itself a constraint. And if compute can't be fed anyway, extra bandwidth wastes power.

⭐ So you were right: the grade is chosen by the buyer. JEDEC sets the generation's ceiling, DRAM makers bin by what parts sustain, and NVIDIA / Google each pick a point within their own power, thermal, reliability and supply constraints, then write it into the spec sheet.
So v7 at 7.2 and GB200 at around 7.8 are two trade-offs, not a capability gap. The cleanest case of the opening line, “the spec sheet is the first thing to see through”: the bandwidth on a spec sheet is the result of a trade-off, not a physical constant.
⭐ Second question: 8 TB/s each way, or shared read/write? Shared. HBM's data lines (DQ) are bidirectional: the same pins carry a read one cycle, a write the next (not full duplex), and each direction switch costs a bus turnaround. (HBM has always used a parallel bidirectional bus, per architecture surveys; industry calls it half-duplex.)

⭐ Two consequences for this lecture:
① Counting reads and writes together is right. The 6 bytes of a vector add = read a 2 + read b 2 + write y 2: one shared bandwidth. Numerator and denominator must match; here they do.
② It explains why fusion is worth so much. Writing an intermediate to HBM and reading it back uses the same bandwidth both ways: you pay twice. Fusion waives both: you save “two trips,” not “half.”

The figure continues below. The division works at every level; this course is about moving data between them. For now: the closer to compute, the lower the line. It pays off with fusion at section's end.

Three uses of the line. Both examples skip attention on purpose: Section 2's first figure derives it; doing it now would spoil it.

1.2 Square is a special case: the smallest dimension sets intensity

The matmul above is square (all sides N), giving N/3. Real ones are M×K · K×N, three lengths. Which sets intensity?

Same division. The operation count is 2·M·N·K, and the bytes moved are 2·(MK + KN + MN). It simplifies cleanly: 1/intensity = 1/M + 1/N + 1/K.

Reciprocals add, so the smallest dominates. “Longer K, higher intensity” is true but capped: as K → ∞, intensity only reaches MN/(M+N). K can't rescue a small M or N.
⛔ The harshest case: batch = 1 decode, M = 1, so 1/intensity ≥ 1: intensity caps at 1, however large K and N. That one line of arithmetic pins LLM decode to bandwidth.

Attention: in QKT both outer dimensions are the sequence length S, and the contraction dimension is head_dim. Most models use 128, so intensity is ≈ 128: below v7's 312 line and v6e's 560.

So “attention is a matmul, hence compute-bound” is a myth. Unfused, it is memory-bound, held there by head_dim.
What does Flash change? Next section's first figure. The direction: it saves no FLOPs; it changes the denominator.
⭐ The same 128 bites again: the 256 × 256 MXU is fed only 128 (§3.4 / §3.6). Intensity asks “wait for data?”; filling asks “is the unit full?”

You now have a ruler. It answers one thing: bandwidth- or compute-bound?
Next, a real op, and the lecture's first big number: fusion changes intensity 1,000×.

Over inter-chip bandwidth, the same division gives 5,768 (tokens each chip needs per step; expand)

The ruler does more than judge ops. Put inter-chip bandwidth under compute, and the division answers a new question: the fewest tokens per chip per step that let cross-chip communication keep up with compute.

Worked for TPU v7 (both numbers on Figure T-1):
2,307 TFLOP/s ÷ 400 GB/s (one axis, bidirectional) ≈ 5,768
All three axes triple bandwidth, cutting the threshold to ≈ 1,922. A full 9,216-chip domain needs a global batch of about 17.7M tokens so communication doesn't drag. Hence huge training batches: not for convergence, but so the network keeps up.

⚠️ The denominator's basis is easy to get wrong. The number above uses one axis bidirectional, 400 GB/s (six links, 1,200 ÷ 3 axes), not the chip's full 1,200. Change the basis and the answer moves 3×; both versions read fine on paper.

⭐ So this section's real output is the division, not 312. Over HBM bandwidth it judges ops; over inter-chip bandwidth, parallelism strategy. The latter belongs to Topic 5; here we just show the ruler can measure something else.

What is that on-chip memory, and “why not keep it in registers?” (two follow-ups; expand)

The place it lands has a name: on GPU it's shared memory, up to 227 KiB; on TPU it's VMEM. HBM traffic does drop, but the data still lands on chip, where the exchange rate is 64, not 312 (derivation in the lower half of the figure in §1.1).

⛔ So why not just keep it in registers? An SM's register file totals 256 KiB, the same size as shared memory, and every extra register means fewer resident warps. Usually you can't. The numbers are in the SM breakdown figure in §3.2.

Why does 312's numerator count only matrix units? What about CUDA cores and the VPU?

312 is the ridge point of the matrix roofline: the numerator is Tensor Core / MXU peak; the vector units are left out.

Because the ops we judge are almost all matmul FLOPs (attention's two, the MLP's big ones); softmax, norms and other vector work are a FLOP rounding error.

How much smaller are the vector units? Work it out:
GB200: 18,944 CUDA Cores × 2 FLOP/cycle × ≈2.06 GHz ≈ 78 TFLOPS
Against 2,500 on the matrix side, a 32× gap. ⚠️ That clock is derived: NVIDIA hasn't published GB200's boost clock, so we use 2,500 TFLOPS ÷ (606,208 MACs/cycle × 2 FLOP) ≈ 2.06 GHz (606,208 = 148 SM × 4 Tensor Cores × 1,024 MACs/cycle; §3.7 takes this apart.) The lecture uses this number throughout (it retires an earlier 2.03 extrapolated from 1.83; 1.83 is a third-party HGX B200 figure, itself 1.4% off against 2,250).
TPU is the same: one TensorCore's two MXUs together do 262,144 MACs per cycle (131,072 per MXU; not the §3.1 figure's cell count), while the VPU processes 1,024 elements per cycle. Different units, but more than two orders of magnitude apart.

Strictly, element-wise ops should be judged against the vector roofline: its ridge point is 78 ÷ 8 ≈ 9.8, not 312.

⛔ The two rooflines are separate. Don't add the two peaks into one line. Adding them assumes the same FLOPs can feed both units at once. They can't: an element-wise kernel never touches the MXU, and a matmul doesn't occupy the vector unit. Draw both; judge each op by the unit it runs on.
Memory is the same: HBM, L2 and on-chip SRAM each have their own bandwidth, so a rigorous roofline is a family of lines, not one. We use only the HBM line: our one question is must this intermediate go out.
⚠️ Convention: one multiply-accumulate (MAC) counts as 2 FLOPs (multiply plus add), as in vendor peaks. So N×N×N is 2N³, not N³, which gives “intensity = N ÷ 3” above.

But the conclusion doesn't flip. The vector add's 0.17 is 58× below 9.8: still memory-bound. That 1.3 TFLOPS is 0.05% of matrix peak and 1.7% of vector peak. Both look bad; the latter is the fair comparison.

⭐ The real takeaway: weak vector units are not an oversight; they are a design choice both sides share. An op on the vector unit loses twice: once to bandwidth, and even without that limit, the usable compute is only a thirtieth.
This is the root reason fusion is mandatory: not to compute less, but to keep data off this narrow, weak path.

⚠️ On-chip SRAM looks like a few-percent near-tie. It isn't. An easy misjudgment

By total capacity it is GPU 231 MiB vs. TPU 134 MiB, 72% more. Same order of magnitude, so it looks safe to ignore. It isn't. The GPU's lead is almost entirely L2, and L2 is exactly the level the TPU lacks entirely. The gap isn't capacity; it's who controls that space. All three ways of counting are in §3.2b.

§ This cell gets a note: rare three-tier evidence. “A neural-network chip must have hardware for exp / tanh / sin.” Right, but public evidence doesn't go that far:

① It existed once, on paper. TPU v1's diagram has a separate Activation unit, and the 2017 paper mentions on-chip “nonlinear function logic.” Not new on TPU.
② It is still a separate resource class today, with positive evidence. In open-source JAX, Pallas reports a TPU kernel's cost through CostEstimate(flops, transcendentals, bytes_accessed, …)—transcendentals is a peer column beside flops. Were they just “a few more instructions on an ordinary ALU,” they'd be counted in flops.
③ But the unit's name, count and implementation really aren't public. The TPU v4 ISCA paper's full description of a TensorCore: four 128×128 MXUs, a VPU with 128 lanes (16 ALUs per lane), and 16 MiB of VMEM. Whether any of the 16 ALUs does transcendentals, it doesn't say. Google Cloud's architecture docs, JAX's official Pallas hardware reference, and JAX's machine-readable chip spec table all list only MXU / vector unit / scalar unit / SparseCore. Nothing public describes a TPU counterpart to the SFUs' “table lookup + interpolation.”
⚠️ The last point matters most: “not listed” on a spec sheet does not mean “not there” on the chip. A counterexample sits in the same documents: the XLU isn't listed on any official spec sheet either, yet it exists (found in another public source). A spec sheet lists only what it wants you to buy on. So this cell says “a separate resource class, unit not public”, neither “none” nor any detail I can't back with a public source.

Section 2

⭐ Where they split: one load, 4 runtime decisions vs. 0

Same appetite, completely different eating habits.
The difference isn't a missing part. On one load path, one side makes four runtime-only decisions, the other none.
The cache accounts for two. The first: do a warp's 32 addresses coalesce? The last: what to evict on a miss. Every later difference grows from here.

Think for thirty seconds Loading a block from HBM onto the chip sets off a chain of events.
Which can be fixed at compile time? Which are known only at runtime? Count the “only known at runtime” ones first; then we walk both paths.

2.1 Same load, two paths

Skip the specs; follow one load from HBM onto the chip. Count the decisions: who makes each, when.

Decision one is the only one unrelated to the cache.
Coalescing merges memory accesses. On a load, each of a warp's 32 threads computes an address; hardware merges them into the fewest transactions.
Merge quality swings bandwidth 8×, and it's known only at runtime: the compiler can't see how addresses are computed. The TPU skips this: arrays are tiled 8 × 128 at compile time and moved as whole tiles. No 32 addresses to merge.

Where the 8× comes from (sector arithmetic, two lines)

What counts is the sector. An NVIDIA cache line is 128 bytes, split into 4 sectors of 32 bytes, and the sector is the real unit of transfer.

Best case: 32 threads read consecutive 4-byte words = 128 bytes, exactly one cache line. 4 sectors, not a byte wasted.

Worst case: the 32 addresses are scattered (e.g., down a column of a row-major matrix), so each thread hits a different sector: 32 sectors, each fetching 32 bytes to use only 4.
32 ÷ 4 = 8×. You pay full bandwidth and discard seven-eighths of it.

⭐ Hence “access memory contiguously” is lesson one of GPU optimization. It optimizes not latency but how much bandwidth each access costs. Source: NVIDIA's cache organization (128 B line / 32 B sector). Nsight Compute reports this directly as sectors per request. A perfect access scores 4; anything above that is waste.

⭐ The course's central decision: this figure's “4 vs. 0” Red doesn't mean “slow”; it means “known only at runtime.” Hit or miss, page walk, queue position: none is known at compile time.
Green doesn't mean “fast”; it means “fixed when the code was written.”

So the labor splits:
The GPU leaves them to runtime hardware, in practice to the kernel writer.
The TPU has the compiler settle them at compile time, so you live with its quirks.

⭐ Section 0's “hedge at every step” is now literal. It's these four decision points, each a real circuit, asking on every access: coalesced? hit? “Hedge nothing” is literal too: the three compile-time givens.
Sections 3 and 5 all follow from this.

⚠️ Why can the TPU assume “the shape is already right”? Because a vector register and an array's memory layout share one shape. Data is used on arrival, no relayout. The cost isn't a non-contiguous row (that's the upside: each segment fills all 128 lanes); it's that the shape is nailed down. A new innermost dimension moves real data, uneven sizes need padding, outside handoffs need relayout. §3.3 has the numbers.

2.3 The main example: why FlashAttention

With the criterion and coordinates set, we run one op end to end. Why FlashAttention? Every large model runs it, and it sits on the wrong side of the 312 line, so both sides must act.

Panel ③ is what matters. “Who schedules the movement” is the previous figure's decision. On the 312 line, the bill is absurd:

So both sides must tile and rewrite. The rest of the course is that rewrite, side by side.

⭐ Side by side: same attention, identical FLOPs to the last MAC, 1,024× apart in intensity.
So intensity is set by the implementation, not just the math. That licenses every later optimization: if it were intrinsic, only new hardware could help. Because implementation sets it, rewriting pays.

⭐ Does it clear the on-chip bar too? Same division, new denominator (Answer: only if tiles have Br ≥ 64 rows. Expand for the math.)
“Crossing to the right” above means the HBM line (312).
But there is a second, on-chip line: shared memory at 64, the last step of Section 1's staircase.
⚠️ Not the 64 above. The axis's 64 is naive attention's intensity; this 64 is the shared-memory threshold. One is the op's, one the hardware's: pure coincidence.
Fusion moves bytes from HBM onto the chip, so divide again with the new denominator.

Let a tile have Br rows and Bc columns, with head_dim d.
Each step reads a K tile and a V tile from shared memory, Bc × d each; the Q tile stays in registers.
Compute: 2 matmuls, 4 × Br × Bc × d FLOPs.
Movement: 4 × Bc × d bytes (bf16).
Cancel terms, and on-chip intensity ≈ Br, the tile's row count.

Br = 128: 128 > 64, clears the bar.
Br = 32: 32 < 64, memory-bound again, this time on-chip.
That answers Section 1's “why still hit the wall?”: it depends on tile size.

⭐ External anchor: real FlashAttention kernels always use 64 or 128 rows per tile. No coincidence: this division forces it.

⚠️ Counts only shared memory, not softmax vector math or register traffic. Order of magnitude, not exact.

TPU: same method. Numerator 1,153.5 (per core: VMEM is 64 MiB/core, so the denominator is per core too; don't pair it with the per-chip 2,307); the denominator becomes VMEM bandwidth, which isn't published, so we won't guess it. Direction only: on-chip bandwidth is an order of magnitude above HBM's, so the threshold is an order lower, in the tens, like the GPU's 64. The TPU's workbench is 64 MiB (289× the GPU's 227 KiB), so tiles can be far larger; its limit isn't this line but §3.4's blade width.
⭐ Look back: that was operator fusion The last section's line, first put to real use.
Flash fuses “scores → softmax → × V” into one kernel, so the 32 GiB intermediate is never written out.
⭐ It saves not one MAC: panels ① and ② are identical. All the savings are in the denominator.
It's the last section's “push the op right,” a thousandfold.
So the question isn't “fuse?” but “who fuses?”
Here a person wrote Flash. Section 5 asks whether it must be a person.
Does fusion trade saved movement for extra FLOPs, and are they “useful”?

Fair question, with a standard answer. Extra compute comes in three very different kinds:

① Recomputation: the same operations, done again. Flash's forward has none. Panels ① and ② have equal MAC counts, a rarity. But the backward does: the unstored intermediate is rebuilt from Q, K. Saved memory is bought with recompute.

② Padding: the zeros added when shapes don't align. They take on-chip space and pass through the matrix unit but produce nothing. The worst of the three: it buys nothing at all. Section 3 shows how much.

③ Extra vector work: online softmax rescales the running result every tile. It isn't much by count, but it lands on the vector unit, which has under 1/30 of the matrix unit's compute (worked out at the end of Section 1). Counting FLOPs underestimates it; you only see it when you count time.

“Useful” has a formal answer: see Section 6 In short: count only the ops the model's math needs and you get MFU; count every op the hardware executes and you get HFU. Under MFU, recomputation and padding never count as useful.
Why it matters, how far apart they get, what to ask before comparing chips: all in Section 6, where they belong (it asks whether two numbers are comparable at all).

So is the trade worth it? Section 1's line earns its keep again, but first, one point made precise.

⭐ Arithmetic intensity's numerator is FLOPs executed, not FLOPs the model needs. Hardware can't tell recomputation apart. So which side of 312 you land on is set by the intensity including recomputation and padding.

But what you care about is useful FLOPs ÷ time. Together that gives two ceilings; the lower wins:

Useful throughput = min(peak × useful fraction, bandwidth × useful intensity) The first term is the compute side: if half the FLOPs are recomputation, it halves.
The second is the bandwidth side: recomputation doesn't change the bytes moved, so it can't help.
⭐ They cross exactly where intensity including recomputation = 312. So the ridge point stays at 312.

Example: intensity with recomputation 600; half the FLOPs are recomputation.
Useful fraction = 1/2 → compute ceiling = 50% of peak; useful intensity = 300 → bandwidth ceiling = 300 ÷ 312 = 96% of peak. The smaller wins: only half the roofline.

⚠️ Easy slip: bandwidth isn't saturated here. You're compute-bound, so movement waits on compute; bandwidth used is only 312 ÷ 600 ≈ 52%. The matrix unit is 100% busy, half on garbage, while bandwidth idles. The classic fingerprint of overdoing the trade.

⭐ So where should trading recompute for traffic stop? When memory-bound, extra compute is free: not cheap, free. It hides in the wait for data. Past 312, it cuts output proportionally, at once. No transition zone: a cliff, not a sliding rate.
The rule: trade until intensity including recomputation just reaches 312, then stop.
If useful intensity is already above 312 (a large matmul), you're compute-saturated: add no recomputation at all.

⛔ But don't remember it as “intensity shouldn't go much above 312.” Higher useful intensity is always better, no limit: a side-4096 matmul has intensity 1,365, zero waste, 100% of peak. Only the intensity you manufactured yourself should sit right at 312.

Finally, back to Flash: it is nowhere near that bad case. Forward is two matmuls, backward four; not storing the intermediate matrix costs backward one more, 7 versus 6 in total. That is HFU ÷ MFU = 1.167, or a useful fraction of 85.7%.

Data movement drops to 1/1,024. 17% more compute buys three orders of magnitude less traffic. Flash didn't just “optimize a kernel”; it changed the op's bound.

Section 3a

Taking it apart: one complexity, two homes

§2 counted decision points: 4 vs. 0. The first half drills inward: chip → core → floor plan → parallel levels → what one instruction consumes.
At each level: what does each side lack or add, and whose decision caused it?
The second half reassembles them and runs FlashAttention on both, side by side.

3.1 Whole chip first: one hides the seam, one hands it to you

Both chips are dual-die packages. One difference shows only at the package; skip to the core and you miss it.

Same build, two presentations Hiding a cost doesn't remove it. You pay without seeing the bill.
This hide-or-expose split recurs at every level. Section 5 prices it.
⭐ Why hiding the seam needs an extra-wide die-to-die link (Bottom line: the 8× isn't a process gap but the price of the “behave like one chip” promise. Expand for the math.)
Two numbers, about 8× apart:
• B200 die-to-die link: 10 TB/s (NVIDIA public figure)
• TPU v7 D2D: 6 × one ICI link (200 GB/s bidirectional each), so ~1.2 TB/s (spec is a multiple of ICI; converted with the course's usual ICI figure)

⚠️ Don't read this as “whose process is better”—the 8× buys two different things.

The reason: the link carries not data but a promise: to everything above, the two dies behave as one chip.
Under it, any access to the other die crosses this link: cache-miss territory, unknowable at compile time. So it's built for an anytime worst case, nearly as wide as on-chip cache bandwidth.

The side that hands you the seam makes no such promise: crossing dies is a compile-time scheduled, avoidable action, not an accident—the link carries only planned ones. Lower demand, narrower link.
v7's link mainly carries the back-and-forth of one tensor-parallel dimension, schedulable in advance, not random bursts.

⭐ The 8× is not a process gap but the price of that promise. The cost is symmetric: one side never thinks about it (but still pays that 21 → 16.8, visible in no API); the other must (but can measure and route around it). ⚠️ Sourcing: 10 TB/s is NVIDIA's public figure; v7's “6 × one ICI link” comes from an internal architecture review; we found no official public source. Shipping the product didn't publish the number. Course rule: such a number gets a source or is marked unsourced. This one is marked.
⚠️ Don't multiply the figure's 131,072 (two MXUs' cell count) straight into peak FLOP/s (Skip “2 MACs per cell per cycle” and you get exactly half. Expand.)

It counts cells: two MXUs, 2 × 256² = 131,072 in all.
But each cell does 2 MACs per cycle; the figure omits this.
⚠️ “2 MACs” isn't “a multiply + an add.” One MAC is itself multiply + add: a × b + c, one cycle, 2 FLOP.
So “2 MACs per cell per cycle” = 4 FLOP, not 2. Miss it: off by 2×.
Common error, 1 MAC/cell/cycle: 131,072 × 2 core × 2 FLOP × 2.2 GHz = 1,153 TFLOP/s, half the header's 2,307. “2 per cell” is missing.
§3.4 walks the full chain.

3.2 Inside a core: five missing pieces, one decision

One level deeper. First what the GPU has, then what the TPU lacks. Reversed, the TPU looks like a “simplified” GPU.

Pause here: the course's key contrast The TPU's five missing parts weren't saved; they became unnecessary.
With no runtime task switching, warp schedulers, scoreboards, dozens of warp slots, resident contexts, dynamic branching: all moot.

Where did the saved area go? Not into more compute or on-chip memory. Tables in §3.7 and §3.2b settle it: the GPU has 16% more total MACs and 72% more on-chip SRAM.
It went into absence itself: no cache or scheduler, and the same compute in 4 big blocks, not 592 small ones: 148× fewer control interfaces (592 vs. 4). ⚠️ Power and yield gains? We haven't measured either; official sources cover part (see fold-out).
Official source: the first TPU paper (ISCA 2017) argued this, and why it fails ten years on (quotes + four caveats)

The paper lists the omissions in one sentence (Jouppi et al., ISCA 2017, In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit, arXiv:1704.04760, p. 8):

the single-threaded TPU has none of the sophisticated microarchitectural features that consume transistors and energy to improve the average case but not the 99th-percentile case: no caches, branch prediction, out-of-order execution, multiprocessing, speculative prefetching, address coalescing, multithreading, context switching, and so forth. Minimalism is a virtue of domain-specific processors.

What the savings became, per the abstract:

The lack of such features helps explain why, despite having myriad MACs and a big memory, the TPU is relatively small and low power.

⭐ The hardest number is in the Figure 2 floor plan: die area is data buffers 37% · compute 30% · I/O 10% · control logic just 2%. The next sentence:

Control is much larger (and much more difficult to design) in a CPU or GPU.

“Simple” on a floor plan: 2%.

On “stability,” the official word differs: not yield but deterministic execution. The paper argues CPU/GPU time-varying optimizations (caches, out-of-order execution, multithreading) help average throughput, not tail latency; TPU determinism better fits their 99th-percentile response time targets. ⚠️ No source found on yield/reliability, so no such claim.

⛔⛔ Four caveats for any citation of this paper ① It compares TPU v1 (2015) with the K80 (2014). Then the savings did become compute: a small die packed 25× the MACs, 3.5× the on-chip memory, at under half the K80's power.
⭐ But for v7 vs. B200, the conclusion flips: §3.7's accounting table puts total MACs at 606,208 vs. 524,288; the GPU has 16% more. Same mechanism (minimalism), different outcome a decade on.
The only defensible claim today: “what's saved is complexity,” not “the savings became compute.” Our opening once made that mistake, recalling the 2017 result. The constraint lifted a generation later; the conclusion stayed.

② Ironwood's official “2×” perf/watt is vs. the previous TPU (Trillium), not GPUs. (Google blog, 2025-04-09; peak FP8 flops per watt of per-chip TDP.) Using it against a GPU swaps the denominator.

③ ⛔ “So how much area was actually saved?” Public information can't answer this. NVIDIA publishes 208B transistors for B200 on two reticle-limit dies (~800 mm² each); Google never publishes TPU die size or transistor count. With only one side publishing, “whose die is smaller” has no common basis.
⭐ But the savings can be itemized, from this course's own two tables: TPU has no L2 at all (126 MB on B200), nor a register file for thread contexts (37 MiB on B200): 157 MiB of on-chip SRAM, spent on two things the TPU lacks entirely; plus 148× fewer control interfaces (592 Tensor Cores vs. 4 MXUs, a gap of 588: 148 is the ratio, not the gap). SRAM and control interfaces both take area. Only “whose chip is bigger” has no answer.

④ Yield and reliability: no citable source, so no claim. The official claim is “deterministic execution,” meaning predictable tail latency, not reliability. Full paper excerpts (all omitted features, the 2% floor plan, all v1-era results) are in L300 §3.2's fold-out.
Contrast notes: the five components, and the most-confused number
📖 Five parts above are for contrast only, not explained Topic 2 asks how the two differ, not how a GPU works inside. Five index entries are folded below.
Where to read about these five in the GPU Microscope (reference · skip when presenting)

① Warp scheduler: the part, GPU Microscope Section 2; at work, Section 7 (“Hiding latency: one swaps workers, one plans shifts”).
② Which silicon a thread / warp is pinned to: Section 3, each abstraction layer matched to silicon.
③ How an SM uses registers: Section 2. Preview: 256 KiB / SM split four ways, 64 KiB per processing block, ≤ 255 registers per thread; so large not for speed but to hold dozens of contexts at once.
④ How L2 is used: capacity and partitions, Section 1; a value's stops between HBM and the MAC units, Section 6.
⑤ How SMs cooperate: Section 3, clusters / distributed shared memory; it exists because the 148 SMs have no fast path between them but L2. The SM figure's cta_group::2 is a tighter tier: two SMs' Tensor Cores team up on one matmul.

⚠️ An easy number to mix up (the next table uses it) B200's L2 is 126 MB (63 MB per die, 4 partitions chip-wide). Not thirty-something MB.
That's the chip's total shared memory, 148 SM × 228 KiB = 33,744 KiB, about 33 MiB.
Nearly 4× apart, and they differ in kind by this course's very decision: L2 is managed by hardware; those 33 MiB, by software.

Next: on-chip real estate. §3.6's whole fusion payoff comes from intermediates staying there. Three questions: how big, how fast, how long you wait, a subsection each.

3.2b “But the GPU has more on-chip memory”: by what measure?

Fair challenge. Every on-chip SRAM on both chips, none skipped:

Capacities from the two Microscopes' source notes (L2, shared memory: third-party tests/specs; VMEM 64 MiB / core, SMEM 1 MiB / core: JAX open-source code).
⚠️ TPU's SMEM is scalar memory (scalars, DMA descriptors), not CUDA's shared memory; in this table VMEM is the counterpart. Totals are our sums: 37+37+37+126 MB→120 MiB = 231 MiB; 64×2+1×2+1×2×2 = 134 MiB.

Same table, three yardsticks, three conflicting verdicts ① Total capacity: GPU wins, 231 vs. 134, 72% more. True; don't argue.
② Software data scratchpad (the “software-managed scratchpad” row only): TPU wins, 130 vs. 37, about 3.5×. The earlier “saved area went into on-chip scratchpad” meant this, unstated, so reading it as ① was fair.
⚠️ This excludes the “matrix operand staging” row. By “who decides,” TMEM's 37 and accumulators' 4 are software-managed too; with them, 134 vs. 74, 1.8×. §3.6 cites the first. Quote ratios with their rows.
③ Contiguous workbench per compute unit: TPU wins by 289×. 64 MiB ÷ 227 KiB ≈ 289. The GPU's 37 MiB isn't one block but 148 mutually invisible 256 KiB islands, L1 taking part of each: one thread block can explicitly manage at most 227 KiB.
⚠️ The 64 MiB is the total floor space, not a one-shot budget The table compares capacity. The 289× hides a caveat: one op's VMEM use has a separate cap.

XLA gives each instruction or fusion its own “scoped VMEM limit,” set by the target chip plus a tunable flag (xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib; raising it when things don't fit is routine). The compiler tiles against this limit, not the 64 MiB.
Other tenants share the space: the pass that picks VMEM-resident tensors, and double buffering (prefetching the next tile).

⭐ 64 MiB caps how big a tile could be; the scoped limit sets this one's size. ⚠️ The default is unconfirmed and may vary by generation, so we name the gate, not a number. Measure on your target.
Two traps: the 289 is a cap divided by a cap, and ① misleads most (expand before quoting)
⚠️ The 289 is a cap over a cap: both “exclusives” are inflated The GPU's 227 KiB is not “one Tensor Core's workbench.” It's the cap one thread block can request; the SM has 4 Tensor Cores, maybe other resident blocks: all compete for that space. (Per-SM shared memory sizes: 0/8/16/32/64/100/132/164/196/228 KiB. 228 is the largest; a thread block can explicitly manage 227.)
Nor is the TPU's 64 MiB all yours. Officially, Ironwood has 64 MB of VMEM per TensorCore (two per chip, hence 128 MB/chip); the 64 is split between the current step and prefetching the next weights. How it's split is set by a flag (xla_tpu_scoped_vmem_limit_kib). ⚠️ The default is unpublished; official tutorials often set it to 65536 (= 64 MiB), implying a much lower default.

⭐ Read precisely, 289 is: the contiguous scratchpad one kernel instance can own, as a ratio of upper bounds. It still decides how big one fusion can be. But don't read it as “TPU has two orders of magnitude more on-chip memory”; that's yardstick ①'s question, and there the GPU has more.
⭐ Why ①, though correct, is the easiest one to be misled by Almost all the GPU's 97 MiB lead is the L2 row. L2 is also the only cell here you can't arrange: you can't “park” weights in L2, only load and hope they're still there.
Counting L2 as “my on-chip space” is the very mistake we've guarded against since Section 2. Two of Section 2's four runtime decision points (L2 hit, eviction) are about it.

⭐ The three yardsticks aren't interchangeable; pick the one matching your question: for “how much SRAM does this chip have,” ①; for “where can I keep intermediates without spilling to HBM”, only ③. Operator fusion faces that second question every time: in §3.6's side-by-side FlashAttention, this 289× sets each side's tile size.

§3.2b covered size and ownership. The other half is speed, with a result almost everyone guesses wrong.

This row's source, and why we can state it now (provenance · skip in class)

Derivation: 32 banks × 4 B per bank per cycle = 128 B/cycle/SM, × 148 SM × 1.83 GHz = 34.7 TB/s. 128 B/cycle has third-party backing: a Hopper microbenchmark (arXiv 2402.13499 Table V) measured on H800 shared memory 127.9 and L1 125.8 B/cycle/SM—one ceiling, so one data path. Two more public sources independently give 128.
Cross-generation anchor: the formula gives H100 132 × 128 × 1.755 GHz ≈ 29.7 TB/s; a third party reports ~33 TB/s for H100 (implying ~1.95 GHz): magnitude matches.
⚠️ Two caveats: ① the B200 clock is uncertain (1.83 is a third-party boost figure; another measurement implies ~1.99), hence ≈ 35 TB/s; ② 128 B/cycle is a ceiling, not a guarantee: in the same table the RTX 4090 gets only 63.7 with scalar FP32, 121.2 with FP32.v4; the H800 gets 125.8 with scalar loads. Too-narrow accesses can't saturate it.

Why the TPU row gives a magnitude, not a number (note on figures)
⚠️ Why the TPU row gives a magnitude, not a number VMEM bandwidth is unpublished: the spec page gives capacity only. Officially it's just “significantly higher bandwidth to the MXU than HBM” (Google Developer forum's Ironwood tuning post); we estimate ~an order of magnitude from that, while the GPU's shared memory is 4.3×.
Certain whatever the numbers: each against its own HBM, the TPU's level pulls further ahead. Don't fill in a precise number or integer multiple: HBM bandwidth is public, so a multiple would reveal the number.
⭐ The counterintuitive one: L2 is big, but only 2.6× faster than HBM Most assume a cache is “an order of magnitude faster.” B200's L2 isn't.
L2's value isn't its own speed but skipping an HBM round trip. A hit gets 2.6×; a miss saves nothing and adds a detour.
So “just land it in L2” isn't a reliable strategy: the gain is small and not guaranteed. Two of Section 2's four decision points bet on this 2.6×, and it's only 2.6×.
⚠️ But “2.6×” assumes big transfers, which often fails That's peak bandwidth, reached only in HBM's best case: one large contiguous block at a time.
Each HBM access pays a fixed startup cost (hundreds of ns) and needs a very wide bus fetching in parallel to hit full speed. Small transfers do neither, so effective bandwidth falls 1–2 orders of magnitude below peak.
On-chip levels avoid this: close, fine-grained, nearly free to start.
⭐ The smaller the transfer, the more an L2 hit gains: 2.6× is its lower bound, not its typical value. This recasts §2.1's sector math: contiguous access also makes each transfer big enough, not just avoids waste. The drop varies with HBM generation, vendor and access pattern, so we give the direction, not the curve.
⭐ Why only 2.6×, and the question that flips it Why slow: L2 is shared chip-wide. Shared memory (≈ 4.3×) and VMEM (about an order of magnitude) both beat 2.6× because they sit beside the compute units, each SM reading its own; L2 data crosses the on-chip interconnect. (Architectural reasoning, not measured attribution. Dropping tags and replacement also saves area and power; distance is most of the gap.)

⭐ “2.6×” answers only a narrow question: how much faster is this byte from L2 than from HBM?
Ask instead about bandwidth per byte of capacity, and it flips: L2 gives 2.6× the bandwidth with 1/1524 the capacity. Multiply: L2's bandwidth density is about 4,000× HBM's.
Concretely: reading all of HBM takes 24 ms; all of L2, 6 µs (all L1 + shared memory: 1.1 µs).
⭐ Two numbers, two jobs; don't merge them • “2.6×” guides optimization decisions: L2 hits pay little; don't rely on them. That stands.
• “4,000×” explains the architecture: why the chip centers on on-chip memory.

⭐⭐ Their ratio is exactly the capacity ratio: on-chip memory's whole edge is being small. Fast for being small, close, short-wired, not for being SRAM.
Reversed, it's the course thread: fusable size and fusion payoff are one plot (§3.6's “stovetop”). ⚠️ No TPU ratio (no VMEM bandwidth data). Same trend, more extreme: VMEM > L2 (128 MiB vs. 126 MB); its HBM multiple (Google: “significantly higher”; est. an order up) dwarfs 2.6×.

Both truly fast levels are software-controlled.

Which GPU level is VMEM? None. By behavior, shared memory (software-moved, no tags, never misses); by capacity, L2-class (128 MiB vs 126 MB; the chip's shared memory totals 37 MiB). Precisely: the TPU built shared-memory behavior at L2 size, then deleted the L2 level.

⛔ Don't read this as “the TPU won three rounds” All three leads are real, and each has a price; remember both.
① A big, fast scratchpad, but no safety net. No cache, so nothing covers a wrong guess: a wrong GPU guess slows things a bit; a wrong TPU tiling leaves the chip stalled. This predictability is paid for, not free.
② The GPU's 37 MiB register file + 37 MiB TMEM look “not spent on data,” but they buy something: irregular shapes, varying lengths and unpredictable branches still run decently. On a TPU, the same work needs fixed shapes first. Section 5 does that math.

⭐ So the conclusion isn't “whose on-chip memory is better.”
Both handle the same thing, uncertainty, in different places.
The GPU spends silicon to absorb it: caches, fallbacks, schedulers.
The TPU eliminates it at compile time; the saved silicon became less circuitry, not more compute (§3.7 counts it). The price: you (or the compiler) commit up front.
Choosing hardware: regular, predictable work suits the TPU; irregular, dynamic-length work justifies the GPU's insurance premium. Section 5 prices that premium.
Two FAQs: can a die use the other die's L2? How do SMs swap data?

① L2 isn't “split in half per die”; it's 4 partitions, two per die (twice Hopper's count). A die uses the other die's L2 with no effort from you: NV-HBI (10 TB/s) joins the dies into one CUDA device with globally coherent L2. The cost is in the table: 21 drops to 16.8, and latency rises. §3.1's “you pay, you just don't see the bill,” made concrete. The TPU is the opposite: two halves, 2 devices; using the other half is an explicit step you write.

② SMs exchange data in three very different tiers: In a cluster (≤ 8 blocks, opt-in 16 since H100, same GPC): distributed shared memory, reading and writing other blocks' shared memory directly, bypassing L2. Blackwell adds a tighter tier, cta_group::2: two SMs' Tensor Cores on one matmul. Outside a cluster, only L2 and HBM: no other fast on-chip path, so sync goes through atomics, cooperative groups, or splitting the kernel.

⭐ Remember the direction of cause and effect: clusters were invented precisely because the 148 SMs have no path between them but L2. It's a layer wedged in between “one SM” and “the whole GPU.” The TPU doesn't need it: a chip has only 2 TensorCores, so core groups never come up. Few cores remove a whole abstraction layer: scale, not design skill.
More detail in GPU Microscope Section 3.

3.2d Latency: the same load, 30 cycles to 659

§3.2b asked “how big,” §3.2c “how fast.” One axis remains: how long you wait. It's the one the GPU itself can't answer.

The question: a warp needs data; not in L1 → check L2 → not there either → fetch from HBM. How long does the chain take?

⛔ The easiest mistake: these segments don't add up “An L1 lookup takes time, L2 more, the HBM fetch more still”: this double-counts.
659 cycles is one full miss, issue to data, measured end to end. The L1 and L2 misses are inside those 659.
Remember the swing, not the sum: one instruction, 30 to 659 cycles.
⭐ So how do you plan? The GPU doesn't “Every case differs, so you can't schedule ahead”: right. The GPU's answer isn't “I can predict it” but “I don't need to.”

None of its three remedies predicts latency:
• Oversubscription: dozens of warps resident per SM; when one stalls, switch. Latency isn't eliminated; other work covers it.
• Scoreboard + dynamic issue: hardware issues each instruction at runtime once its operands arrive.
• The cache is a guessing machine: it bets you'll reuse the data.

The TPU deletes the uncertainty at the source. No hardware cache → no misses → no variable latency. Data sits in VMEM not by luck but because the compiler's DMA put it there; it knows which cycle to wait on.

⭐ In one line: the GPU hides uncertain latency behind other work; the TPU deletes the uncertainty. One answer is statistical, the other deterministic.
So lacking L2 isn't a missing feature: a machine scheduled to the cycle at compile time needn't guess.
⭐ Also why the two sides' “tuning” shares nothing On a GPU you tune for “enough other work”—occupancy, resident warps per SM, coalescing, trading registers for warps.
On a TPU you tune for “room for the compiler to schedule”—dimension alignment, tiling, enough double buffering, scoped vmem size.
Same word, no overlapping knobs. So experience barely transfers. Not because it's hard: your knobs don't exist on the other side.
⚠️ Not drifting apart; quite the opposite Modern CUDA kernels are moving toward the TPU. Async copies, TMA, explicit barriers: peak kernels like FlashAttention now issue their own async transfers, double-buffer and wait on their own.
That's a hand-written static schedule on the GPU. At peak, “guessing” isn't enough.
⭐ It returns in §3.5's further reading (Blackwell's matmul moves the accumulator out of registers, single-thread issue): same direction, two components.

3.3 Parallel hierarchy: which levels are set at runtime

First, two coordinate terms. This section and §3.4 rely on them, and both names mislead:

The die lost components. One level up, the programming model loses things too: same cause, again.

It comes down to one question.

⭐ Where everything starts Writing GPU code, you don't know which SM your work lands on, or when.
Hardware decides at runtime.

So you can't name anything. You can't write “SM 3, do this.”

Think for thirty seconds If you can't name the hardware, what can you still tell it? Hint: all you still know is how the pieces of work relate to each other.

All you can do: describe relationships. What must stay together, what can land anywhere.

The batch that “must stay together” is a block.

Why “must”? Because its pieces swap intermediate results,
in the SM's own small local memory.
Once a batch lands on an SM it can't move, or the intermediates are lost.

Work that never talks can land anywhere; all of it is the grid.

These two levels are yours. Your code says two things: these go together; this many in total.

Hardware has its own groupings, for another reason: saving circuitry.

Instruction fetch is costly. So 32 data elements share one.
That bundle of 32 is a warp. The number is fixed in silicon.

Four levels: bottom two fixed by hardware, top two set by you.

Two more came later, each forced by a specific problem:

warpgroup: newer matrix instructions are shaped for four warps issuing at once.
cluster: neighboring SMs want direct access to each other's local memory, no detour.

All six side by side, and what forced each.

⭐ The takeaway Trace those problems one step further back.
All six levels grow from the opening “you don't know.”
Runtime placement is why you need a language for who must be together, who sees whom.

The TPU fixes everything at compile time. No “you don't know.”

It needs not one level of that language.

The two sides' levels answer different questions. GPU levels describe who must be together; the TPU never needs to.
So the table below is ordered by question.

CUDA's full nesting thread → warp → (warpgroup) → block → cluster → grid is folded below for reference. What to remember: the three “mismatches” after it.

Full six-level nesting table (reference · skip in class)
LevelSizeSet byMaps to
thread1— 1 lane in a sub-core
warp32 threads Fixed in hardware, not yours 1 of 4 sub-partitions (sub-cores)/SM
warpgroup4 warps = 128 threads Fixed by the ISA One warp from each of 4 sub-partitions
block (thread block)
(= CTA)		 ≤ 1,024 threads = ≤ 32 warps You, in code All on one SM; never migrates
