⭐ Skip the nesting; remember three mismatches ① An SM hosts several blocks. A block caps at 32 warps; an SM has 64 warp slots (= 2,048 threads), so blocks share an SM, blind to each other's shared memory. §5.1's “occupancy” counts filled slots of the 64.
② A warpgroup is an instruction unit, not a scheduling unit. Nothing “schedules a warpgroup”; it's the shape wgmma/TMEM need four consecutive warps to issue together. Hence §3.4's trend of matrix instructions mobilizing ever more threads, until Blackwell's tcgen05 reverses it: a single thread issues it.
③ The cluster came later, for §3.2c's reason. The 148 SMs connect only through L2; a cluster lets blocks in one GPC read and write each other's shared memory directly, bypassing L2. The TPU needs none: a chip has just two TensorCores.

⭐ Rule of thumb: hardware fixes the first three levels' boundaries; your code sets the last three's sizes. What each level shares, how it syncs: GPU Microscope, Figure G-3.
Origins of three names: warp / CTA / warpgroup (etymology; open only if the figure didn't land)

Warp comes from weaving: on a loom, the warp is the lengthwise threads pulled together, parallel strands that move as one. The threads are, literally, bound together.

Why 32? Wider amortizes fetch/decode better, but divergence costs more, coalescing coarsens. AMD long used 64 (the wavefront); newer designs went back to 32.

CTA stands for Cooperative Thread Array, and it is the thread block: CUDA calls the level a block; PTX and the hardware call it a CTA.

warpgroup does more than issue wgmma; it enabled warp specialization: one warpgroup only moves data from HBM to shared memory, the others only issue matrix instructions. Split movers from computers and the pipeline overlaps. FlashAttention-3 builds on this: the GPU side's shape in §3.6.

Deeper still. “An SM” has been a black box. Open it and the numbers above need no memorizing.

What a thread owns, what it shares (expand)
⭐ What a thread owns, what it shares It owns none of the compute units.
CUDA and Tensor Cores belong to no one; they're pipeline slots. This cycle's issuing warp uses them; next cycle, another.
Tensor Cores more so: a whole warp (four from Hopper on) issues one instruction; “a thread's Tensor Core” doesn't exist.

It truly owns its registers, plus its batch's share of shared memory.
A batch claims them on landing, returns them when done, never moves them between.

⭐ This explains two things.
Registers never move, so swapping warps is free: the old warp's state stays put.
Owned outright, registers always limit you first, not compute units.
Counting registers: units, limits, why multiples of 8 (reference · skip in class)

A register is 32 bits (4 bytes), the unit of the compiler's “registers per thread.” Check: 65,536 × 4 B = 256 KiB, the register file in the figure.

Per-thread cap: 255 on current GPUs (it has changed; early parts had 63), the figure's “255 per thread (max)” row. ⚠️ NVIDIA disagrees with itself: the Programming Guide says 255, CUDA's own cuda_occupancy.h says 256 from Volta on. I couldn't confirm the hardware truth (likely “256 allocatable, 255 usable,” my guess). Use 255.
Registers are allocated per warp, in units of 256, unchanged from Kepler to Blackwell: take “registers per thread × 32,” round up to a multiple of 256.
Per thread: round up to a multiple of 8. So shaving a register or two often changes nothing; you must cross a multiple of 8. Source: code, not docs; cuda_occupancy.h lists these per compute capability.

64-bit values take two registers: doubles, pointers. Extra pointers cut occupancy fast.

Last, the bottom row.

A warp is 32 threads. Each has an index in the warp, 0 to 31. That position is a lane.

So the GPU has lanes too. In hardware a lane is a SIMD channel, same as a TPU lane.

The only difference: GPU lanes have names; TPU lanes don't.

A GPU lane has a writable index. Give it its own if and loop, like a real thread.
A TPU lane is out of reach: you can't write “lane 37, do something else”.
The vector moves as one; the compiler maps elements to lanes.

So a CUDA “thread” isn't your usual thread. To pin it down, set it between its two neighbors.

3.3a What one lane does in a real matmul

“A thread is a lane” is abstract. Ground it in a real matmul, one era at a time; mixing them confuses.

① Classic, no Tensor Cores. A thread owns one output cell (or a small tile). It runs its own K loop: loads A and B slices from shared memory into its own registers, multiply-accumulates, holds the sum, writes it back. It moves data and computes: most people's picture.

② Modern, with Tensor Cores: that picture is void. The matrix instruction is one instruction issued by the whole warp, on a fragment: one tile's elements, spread over 32 threads' registers in a fixed, PTX-defined layout.
In a typical m16n8k16, each thread holds 8 fp16 of A, 4 fp16 of B and 4 fp32 of accumulator C.
⭐ No thread computes a full output element alone. Results return as a scattered fragment.

A whole warp issues each Tensor Core instruction, so “which cell does this thread own?” is meaningless.
A thread is just a register holder and 1/32 of an issue. That's what “a thread is really a lane” means.

⭐ Is it SIMD? Two levels, two answers Hardware: yes. A warp's 32 lanes share fetch, decode and issue and run the same instruction each cycle. That's SIMD hardware.
Programming model: no. You write scalar code per thread, and since Volta each thread has its own program counter and branches.

⭐ So SIMT = scalar code on SIMD hardware. The cost: divergent branches take turns. They look independent but queue. ⚠️ Separate layer: a thread can also use vector instructions (128-bit loads). That's SIMD within a thread, not warp-level.

All this (you write scalar; hardware builds SIMD, queues divergence) is the price of runtime adaptation. The TPU skips that decision, so it lacks even the word “thread”: only lanes, never individually commanded.

⭐ Does a thread move data? Yes, but that role is retiring. Pre-Ampere, threads moved data (global → registers → shared), busy meanwhile; Ampere's cp.async goes straight to shared; with Hopper's TMA one thread issues one descriptor per tile; 31 sit out.
In three generations the thread went from “mover + computer” to “register holder.” §3.3b draws this path (three-generation figure); Blackwell then moves the accumulator out of registers into TMEM.

3.3b The runtime-adaptation bill: three circuits

That takeaway is about the programming model: the shape you see in code.

In hardware, the cost is three circuits, each answering one narrow question:

① Who can issue now?
② Who syncs with whom, and how?
③ How does data arrive with threads free?

On the first, we owe you a definition. “Scoreboard” came up several times (opening the SM, pricing exposed lanes) but was never defined.

In one sentence: a scoreboard is a table of whether each instruction's operands have arrived. Each cycle the scheduler scans it and issues a ready warp.
That's runtime-only knowledge of who can run, in silicon: something must record what isn't ready. The TPU has no such table.

How the scoreboard knows a warp is “ready” (mechanism; open if asked)
⭐ Scoreboard: how a warp counts as “ready” NVIDIA didn't coin the name; it dates to the 1964 CDC 6600.
It first let instructions complete out of order, needing a central table of busy units and pending register writes.
Its official name: Scoreboard.

On the GPU, NVIDIA splits instructions by one test: does the compiler know the latency?
The fixed-latency half needs no tracking: an FMA takes fixed cycles, so the compiler writes “stall N cycles” into the instruction; hardware obeys. Hence the control bits on every SASS instruction.
The variable-latency half is the scoreboard: memory, special functions, matrix ops (latency unknown at compile time). Each warp has six counters (SB0–SB5): a producer bumps one at issue, drops it at writeback; a consumer's 6-bit mask names which must hit zero.

⭐ Not a big table of dirty registers, but six tiny counters plus compiler-planted markers, answering: can this warp issue now? Latency hiding rests on it: without it, no warp swapping.

📌 A diagnostic: Nsight's long / short scoreboard stalls split on whether the awaited data leaves the SM: shared memory, special functions, matrix ops are short; global loads, long. Memory-bound kernels: long dominates.
⚠️ Six counters, control-bit format: from third-party microbenchmarks (Analyzing Modern NVIDIA GPU cores, 2025), not official.
Why “score”? And why this isn't the CDC's board (etymology, distinctions · skip in class)

Sourced vs. inferred. Sourced: the term comes from the CDC 6600, whose component was named Scoreboard. I found no source for why the word was chosen; what follows is speculation.

To keep score means not just tallying points but tracking the current state: a scoreboard at a ballpark lets you glance up once and know the situation, as this table does. So read it as “status board,” not points tally. On the GPU, though, the name fits literally: it counts, up on issue and down on writeback; the old board just raised a “busy” flag.

More importantly, the boards differ. The CDC one was a central table tracking hazards on all registers, even write-after-write (WAW: an earlier write landing late over a later one), all checked at runtime.
NVIDIA's has six counters per warp, asking only “is what I'm waiting for back?”; fixed-latency dependencies skip it; the compiler settles those in the control bits.
The name was inherited; the mechanism shrank. A footnote to the course's thread: what compile time can decide shouldn't wait for runtime, and even the GPU is moving that way.

The second: a few hardware barriers in the SM. Warps arrive, hardware counts heads; when full, all go.
Mechanism folded at the end; the practical point:

A warp waiting at a barrier keeps its slot. So all that waiting frees no slots: a sync-heavy kernel's occupancy doesn't improve.

The third gets a figure. Watch which column changes, which never do.

The other two answers: block sync, and how a cluster reads another SM (reference · skip in class)

1. Syncing within a block. Behind __syncthreads() is the SM's small pool of hardware barriers above. Three easily missed points: ① it counts warps, not threads; a warp moves as one; ② it doubles as a memory fence: shared-memory writes before it are visible to all after it, no separate fence; ③ a warp waiting at the barrier still holds its slot. (Already in the main text.)

Ampere added asynchronous barriers, splitting “arrive” from “wait.” A warp says “arrived” without blocking, works on, and waits only when it needs data. Early arrivals don't idle. Hopper lets waiters truly sleep; before, they spun on shared memory.

The two barriers also live in different places. Old bar / barrier: a small fixed SM pool, capped per CTA; mbarrier: a shared-memory object, as many as shared memory holds. Per the PTX docs.

2. How a cluster reads another SM's shared memory. Three things must hold: ① a cluster's blocks are guaranteed co-scheduled by hardware; ② each GPC has a dedicated SM-to-SM network; a cluster must fit in one GPC because that network stops at its edge; ③ cluster.map_shared_rank(ptr, target_rank) gives the other block's address (PTX mapa); plain loads/stores then use it, and the network routes.

⚠️ How near matters more H100 microbenchmarks: own shared memory, 29 cycles; own via the DSM interface, 33 (the extra 4 are the interface; nothing leaves the SM); another SM, 181, ~30% below L2; a global-memory round trip (store + load), 956.

So it does not “merge several SMs' shared memory into one big pool”: 181 cycles is over six times the local 29. A shortcut cheaper than L2: use it to save those 900-odd cycles, not as if it were local.
⭐ Three circuits, one bill Scoreboard: “who can issue now.” Barrier: “who syncs with whom, and how.” TMA: “how data arrives without tying up threads.” Together: the itemized bill for deciding at runtime.

The TPU needs none. Not because it's primitive: it answers all three at compile time. §3.2's five “missing components,” revisited: what's missing is this bill, not capability.

3.3c ⭐ In what order does hardware run a matmul?

Both sides are taken apart. Still unsaid, and more basic: in what order does hardware compute a matmul?

This may be the course's one spot where nearly everyone is wrong without noticing. The wrong version is too natural: it's how you do a matmul on paper.

The picture in your head: left row 1 times right column 1, summed pairwise, gives the top-left entry; that cell is done; next. Mathematically correct. Yet no real hardware, GPU or TPU, works this way.

⛔ Wrong dataflow, not wrong math; spec sheets list only math Inner- and outer-product order give identical results, to the last digit. No wrong answer ever exposes a wrong mental model.
They differ in how much data moves, the half that sets speed.
Inner: 24 reads, 12 MACs. Outer: 12 reads, 12 MACs. That's a 2×2 toy; big tiles make it tens to hundreds of times.
⭐ The equation to take away: accumulators buy reuse Why not just one row of accumulators? One clean equation answers.

For an M×N accumulator tile, each step along K reads one column of A (M values) + one row of B (N values): M + N values. That buys M × N MACs.

⭐ So the reuse factor = M × N ÷ (M + N).
ShapeReuseWork/read
1 × N (one row only)N ÷ (1+N)≈ 1, even at N = 10⁶
128 × 12816,384 ÷ 25664
128 × 25632,768 ÷ 384≈ 85
⭐ The harsh part: it's capped by the short side. Short side 1, long side a million: reuse is still 1. The long side doesn't help.
So an accumulator array doesn't “hold the result”; it buys reuse. Each extra accumulator pairs already-moved operands once more. ⭐ This is Section 1's arithmetic-intensity thread, first cast in silicon.
⭐ The circuit view also demands 2D The MXU is a 256×256 2D array that physically emits 256 partial sums every cycle. One row of accumulators would use 1/256 of the array.
A 2D array needs a 2D accumulator, shaped like the array, not an arbitrary choice.

Follow-up: isn't draining costly too? No. Any tiling drains exactly M×N. The real overpayment is B: row by row, you re-read all of B M times.
⚠️ Two accuracy caveats to keep when presenting ① The GPU column is algorithm-level dataflow. One MMA instruction already reduces a short run of K (16/32/64) inside: same shape, batched. Cross-k-tile accumulation is explicit: the first tile zeroes the accumulator; later tiles add.
② In the TPU column the K sum completes spatially inside the array, needing no external accumulator; external ones serve only across K tiles: real K is often thousands, and the array takes 256 at a time.

⭐ In one sentence: same math; only which dims go to space and which to time differs. It drives everything: accumulator size, the tile as core knob, why the TPU must keep weights still. §3.4 next compares how big a tile one instruction eats: this choice in numbers.

3.4 One instruction's bite: a 16× gap in contraction depth

§3.3 asked who issues the instruction. Now: how big a block does one instruction eat?

An internal detail that decides which head_dim is free.

In both, look at the instruction's depth along the summed dimension.

GPU: 16. TPU: 256. A 16× gap.

That is the contraction dimension: the one a matmul sums away, i.e. terms accumulated per instruction.

One rule for the letters M/K/N: K alone appears twice and alone disappears (summed away). The other two shape the result.

⭐ The trouble with 128: it falls between two stools, too small for the array's edge (half of 256), too few streamed rows to amortize the weight load.

Why: the letters' origin, why N wastes half too, is transposing equivalent? (open if asked)
⭐ Getting M/K/N straight, once Write a matmul as A[M, K] × B[K, N] = C[M, N]. One rule covers all three letters:
⭐ K is the only one that appears twice, and the only one that disappears.
Twice: A's columns must equal B's rows, so it joins the two matrices. Gone: it is summed away, hence “contraction dimension”.

The other two are the result's shape: M = how many result rows, N = numbers per row. K = terms summed into each number.

⭐ With this you can read instruction names: m16n8k64: output 16×8, each number a sum of 64 terms. (The order follows BLAS: output shape M, N first, then K.)
⭐ Where the three letters come from: a triple loop The most naive matmul is three nested loops, by tradition named i, j, k, top to bottom:
for i (each result row) → for j (each number in it) → for k (add term k)

⭐ The three capitals are simply the bounds of the three lowercase loops. M, N, K = trip counts of i, j, k.
k is the innermost loop: it accumulates. So “K = contraction dimension” isn't convention: it names the accumulation loop.

⚠️ Why i/j/k/m/n: the notation comes from Fortran BLAS, and in Fortran, variables starting with I–N are integers by default, so indices and sizes use those six letters. (The usual explanation, not a standard's text; the Fortran rule itself is fact.) ⛔ Don't invent meanings for the letters (M≠Matrix, N≠Number); that makes them harder to remember.
⛔ The real snag isn't the letters, it's the word “rows” “Number of rows” measures a column's length; “number of columns”, a row's length. “M rows” is vertical. Genuinely counterintuitive.

Three reframings, from good to best:
① Not rows and columns: height and width. A is M tall, K wide; B is K tall, N wide. Multiplying needs “A's width = B's height”; result: “A's height × B's width”. No more “row count is column length”.
② Chain the shapes and watch them link. M K · K N → M N: adjacent letters must match, then both vanish. The rest is the answer.
③ ⭐ The most valuable one: M is time; K and N are space. On a systolic array the K×N block is loaded and held: K is the array's height, N its width, both fixed by hardware. M is just how many rows flow through, as long as you like.
⭐ Hence a pattern in this course: K=128 and N=128 each waste half, yet M never comes up: it takes no space, only time.
⚠️ Why does N=128 also keep only half? Same math, different reason Picture the array as a 256 × 256 grid of cells. For A[M,K] × B[K,N], the hardware lays B's K×N block onto the grid (K high, N wide), then streams A's rows in from the left.

A cell does useful work only if both hold:
① data flows into the row above it;
② someone needs the sum accumulated down its column.

⭐ Each kind of waste violates one:
· K=128 (half the height): the bottom 128 rows have no input above them. Fill them with something else? No: a column's cells add into one number, so anything else corrupts it.
· N=128 (half the width): the right 128 columns have no consumer below. They compute output channels nobody needs: your output has 128, no more.

The arithmetic: utilization = (K ÷ 256) × (N ÷ 256). One side at 128 (half), the other full: 50%. ⚠️ Derived from the array structure, not official, but it agrees with the official line: at most 50% at head_dim 128.

⭐⭐ Most important: the two wastes are not equally recoverable.
· N short: recoverable. If another matmul takes the same A, concatenate both B's along the width; one pass. Fusing the Q, K, V projections into one matmul does exactly this: all three take the same X, so their N dims concatenate.
· K short: not recoverable. K is summed: anything concatenated adds into the same result. The core difference from N.

⚠️ In attention, though, the PV step's N=128 is the unrecoverable kind: that needs matmuls sharing a P, and every head's P differs.
⭐ A false rescue, and two real ways out ⛔ First, the idea everyone has: “let all heads share one V?” MQA/GQA do exactly that. But it points the wrong way.
Concatenating N needs “same A, different B”; shared KV gives you “same B, different A”. That stacks only along M, and M is time, not space: stacking never fills that half.
(MQA/GQA save KV-cache memory and bandwidth, not array utilization here. Don't conflate.)

⭐ The two real ways out:
① Change head_dim. At 256, both wastes vanish. But that is a model architecture decision, not a tuning knob. A model's head_dim caps its attention's share of peak here.
② Compute the matmul transposed. PV hits N=128; compute the transpose Vᵀ · Pᵀ instead and all three letters move: M becomes 128; K and N become the two long dimensions.
⭐ This is “M is time, K and N are space” applied directly: move the 128 from space to time. 128 as array width is waste; as “rows flowing through” it costs nothing.
⚠️ Is the transpose still the same computation? Mathematically yes, but it has two costs
It is an identity: (P · V)ᵀ = Vᵀ · Pᵀ. Exact, not an approximation.
① The output is transposed. Either the consumer takes it, or you flip it back, which costs on a TPU (cross-lane moves, VPU work).
⭐ So you need a fully transposed pipeline, not one transposed step: the whole chain stays transposed, or flipping back and forth eats the savings. (Splash Attention's interface makes the Q/K/V layout a parameter, so the choice is yours by design, not hard-coded.)
② Same math ≠ same bits. Accumulation order changes; last bits may differ. Flag it in numerics alignment, or someone burns half a day on a “bug.”
⚠️ Others report it working (one report: efficiency 30-odd → 50-odd percent); we haven't reproduced it. Our three minimal repros were negative, on a baseline 8× off production, so we can neither confirm nor refute. ⛔ Not a conclusion.
Why does Vᵀ · Pᵀ equal (P · V)ᵀ? Step by step (shape → accumulation → numbers → cost)

Step 1: the shapes match.

  • P is [q, kv], V is [kv, d] → O = P·V is [q, d]
  • Vᵀ is [d, kv], Pᵀ is [kv, q] → Vᵀ·Pᵀ is [d, q]

[q, d] transposed is exactly [d, q]: shapes match; now check the numbers inside.

Step 2: cell by cell, the dot product uses the same two vectors.

Original cell: O[i, j] = P's row i (horizontal, length kv) dotted with V's column j (vertical, length kv).

Transposed cell: (Vᵀ·Pᵀ)[j, i] = Vᵀ's row j dotted with Pᵀ's column i.
By definition, row j of Vᵀ is column j of V, column i of Pᵀ is row i of P.

⭐ Both sides dot the same two vectors, just in swapped order.

Step 3 (the crux): why swapping the order changes nothing.

Matrix multiply isn't commutative (A·B ≠ B·A): swapping changes “whose rows pair with whose columns”. But here we transpose both at once; rows and columns swap too.

⭐ The two swaps cancel; the pairing is unchanged. Only the factor order in each term changes. They're scalars; scalars commute.

In one line:
O[i,j] = Σ P[i,k]·V[k,j] and (Vᵀ·Pᵀ)[j,i] = Σ V[k,j]·P[i,k]
Same products, same sum.

Step 4: numbers, matching term by term.

P = [ 1  2  3 ]        V = [  7   8 ]
    [ 4  5  6 ]            [  9  10 ]
                           [ 11  12 ]

O = P·V, top-left: 1×7 + 2×9 + 3×11 = 7 + 18 + 33 = 58

Vᵀ = [ 7  9 11 ]       Pᵀ = [ 1  4 ]
     [ 8 10 12 ]            [ 2  5 ]
                            [ 3  6 ]

Vᵀ·Pᵀ, top-left:   7×1 + 9×2 + 11×3 = 7 + 18 + 33 = 58

⭐ Not a coincidence of totals: the terms 7 + 18 + 33 match one by one. Overall, O = [[58,64],[139,154]], and Vᵀ·Pᵀ = [[58,139],[64,154]], exactly the transpose of O.

Step 5: the amount of compute is identical.

Original: q × d outputs, each kv MACs → q·d·kv.
Transposed: d × q outputs, each still kv MACs → d·q·kv. Not one more or less.

⛔ Then why is it faster? What changes is not the number of MACs but how they are laid out on the 256×256 grid.

  • Original: M=q, K=kv, N=d=128 → only half the array's width is used
  • Transposed: M=d=128, K=kv, N=q → height and width fill; 128 moved to M

⭐ Same MACs, different layout, fewer idle cells. That is all “move the 128 from space to time” means.

⛔ But the transpose isn't free: it swaps costs “M can be as long as you like” covers only the space cost. A large M takes no array space, but a small M has its own cost.

A systolic array doesn't produce results instantly: data flows left to right, partial sums top to bottom; fill + drain take on the order of the array's side length.
Load weights once, stream just 128 rows: head and tail can't be amortized. Negligible over thousands of rows; over 128 it is the main cost. (⚠️ Steady state is full; only head and tail aren't. So: not “never full” but “full too briefly”.)

⚠️ A natural idea that doesn't work: “Then why not stream several heads' P back to back?”
After the transpose, what streams is Vᵀ, and what gets loaded is Pᵀ. But each head's Vᵀ must pair with its own Pᵀ: M can't be concatenated either, for the same reason N couldn't.

⭐ What the transpose really does is trade “half the array idle” for “poor pipeline amortization”. Whether it pays depends on which cost is larger, which paper can't settle.
⚠️ This may be why our three repro rounds came out negative, but that is speculation; this term wasn't measured separately. Not established.
One level deeper: how does the right matrix enter the array? Can both stream? (mechanism)

① Weights are shifted in; filling one tile takes 256 cycles.

Not stamped in at once: weights are pushed down row by row from a FIFO, rolling over the array like a shutter. The first-generation TPU paper: it takes 256 cycles to shift a tile in.

② Must the left matrix wait for the load? Usually not: double buffering.

Each cell has two sets of weight registers: one computes while the other loads the next tile. So the 256 cycles hide behind the previous tile's compute; the paper: “double-buffering (to hide the 256 cycles it takes to shift a tile in)”.

⛔ But hiding has a precondition, and 128 breaks it The condition: computing this tile must outlast loading the next. Loading ≈ 256 cycles; streaming M rows ≈ M cycles.
⚠️ Why does “compute” take only M cycles? Once the array is full, the left matrix advances one row per cycle and a column of results lands each cycle: M rows, M cycles, however many MACs. All 65,536 cells do their MACs simultaneously, at no extra time.

⭐ So at M = 128, compute takes 128 cycles, loading 256. Loading is slower; double buffering can't hide it. You stall on weights.
⚠️ This combines two public numbers (“256 cycles to load a tile” + “B rows take B pipeline cycles”); not an official conclusion, but it makes “a small M has its own cost” computable.

③ Once loaded, how is it “held”? Each cell has one weight register; a value stays put until the whole tile is done. The name: weight-stationary.

④ Can both matrices stream? Yes: one of the three classic dataflows.

They differ only in what stays put in the cells:

  • Weight-stationary (WS): cells hold a block of B, so the array holds K × N; M streams through. The TPU does this.
  • Output-stationary (OS): both matrices stream, A from left, B from top; results build up in place. The array holds M × N; K streams through. Your question.
  • Input-stationary (IS): cells hold a block of A, so the array holds M × K; N streams.

Output-stationary's advantage: no “load weights” step; both operands stream in together. The cost: results pile up in the cells and need a final pass to drain.

⭐⭐ Side by side, the three dataflows expose this section's real problem The three dataflows do one thing: choose which dimension is time.
· Weight-stationary: space is K and N, time is M
· Output-stationary: space is M and N, time is K
· Input-stationary: space is M and K, time is N

head_dim = 128 falls between two stools.
· As a space dimension: it is too small (only half of 256; the other half idles)
· As a time dimension: it is too short (128 cycles can't amortize a 256-cycle load)

⭐ So no dataflow saves it; only moving it does, hence “transpose the matmul”, not “use a different array”. Transposed, though, 128 lands on time and hits the “can't hide” problem above.
⚠️ Self-consistent but not measured: a way to understand it, not a verdict.

One figure, four bands: stationarity, tiling a real size, ping-pong loading, segments vs. reloads.

A real size, start to finish: how the Q projection runs on the MXU (M=128K, K=7168, N=1536)

The three numbers. Left X: [131072, 7168]; right W: [7168, 1536]; result Q: [131072, 1536].

① Block size? No choice: 256 × 256. That is the array's size; the right matrix is cut to it.

② How many tiles in total?

  • K direction: 7168 ÷ 256 = 28
  • N direction: 1536 ÷ 256 = 6
  • In total 28 × 6 = 168 tiles.
⚠️ Two kinds of “moving”: the most common math error · HBM to on-chip: the whole W is only 7168 × 1536 × 2 B = 21 MiB, so it all fits in VMEM in one go (VMEM has 64 MiB). Once.
· On-chip, shifted into the array: 256 cycles every time a tile is used. Over ten thousand times.
When someone says “moving B”, ask which, or you'll be off by orders of magnitude.

③ The timeline. Feed the left matrix in 2048-row segments:

load B(k=0, n=0)       ← 256 cycles; 1st tile waits
      ↓
stream 2048 rows of X  ← 2048 cycles
  (meanwhile load B(k=1,n=0)) ← 256, hidden in 2048
      ↓
stream 2048 rows of X  ← using B(k=1,n=0)
  (meanwhile load B(k=2,n=0))
      ↓
      … after 28 passes …
      ↓
2048 rows × 256 out cols fully accumulated → write
      ↓
n=1: 28 more passes … all six n done → 2048 rows done
      ↓
next 2048-row segment → all 168 B tiles again

④ Does streaming wait for the load? Only on the first tile. Then double buffering overlaps loading the next tile with computing this one. Hiding needs “rows streamed > 256”: here 2048, 8× headroom.

⑤ Is each B tile used only once? No. It is reloaded once per left-matrix segment.

Segment rowsAccumulator B loadsHidden?
2560.25 MiB86,016No (256 ≤ 256)
5120.5 MiB43,008Yes
20482 MiB10,752Yes
81928 MiB2,688Yes

⭐ Why left-matrix segments can't be short: longer segments, fewer B reloads, but the accumulator stays on-chip and grows with them. So on-chip capacity caps segment length: the stovetop again.

⑥ Then stream all of M in one go, loading B only 168 times? No: the accumulator would need 131072 × 256 × 4 B = 128 MiB, more than all of VMEM. So M must be segmented, and segmenting reloads B. Not a weak implementation, just arithmetic.

⭐ This example also proves that a small M costs you Here M has 130K rows; any segment is far over 256, so loading hides. Projection-type matmuls never have this problem.
Transposed attention has M = 128, below even the 256 threshold. Same mechanism, opposite outcomes.

Plug in a real shape to feel the two numbers.

Attention's head_dim is commonly 128.

GPU: 128 ÷ 16 = 8: eight instructions, zero waste.
TPU: 128 against 256: half filled, half empty.

Why not fill the empty half with other work?

You can't. The contraction dimension is an accumulation chain: anything you add lands in the same partial sum.

Why doesn't the GPU pay this?

Not because it has a scheduler. Swapping warps fills time bubbles, not a half-empty contraction dimension.
Its K is only 16; nearly every shape is a multiple of 16.

Price of a K this narrow, aligned at runtime: the five parts §3.2 found the TPU lacks.

⚠️ Top trap: 16 and 256 are instruction shapes, not work per cycle. Divide them and the peak comes out absurd.

Reconciling the peaks; three math traps (to check the numbers)
⛔ The easiest trap: K=16 is one instruction's shape, not one cycle's work Common reasoning: “an instruction is 16 deep, an SM has one Tensor Core: 2,250 TFLOPS can't be.”
Both steps fail: wrong units; instruction shape taken for per-cycle throughput. Details below.
Check: 4,096 × 2 FLOP × 148 SM × 1.83 GHz = 2,219 TFLOPS vs. official 2,250; the 1.4% gap: clock uncertainty, not the formula.

⭐ Instruction shape sets work per instruction (control-overhead amortization); MACs per cycle is set by array size. Don't divide them.
⭐ The TPU peak chain, reconciled the same way The TPU's peak chain is stated verbatim by Google:
262,144 FLOP/cycle/MXU × 2.2 GHz × 4 MXUs = 2,307 TFLOPS
Official: 2,307, exact.
⭐ This also closes the hook from §3.1. The 131,072 in that figure is a cell count (two MXUs); the 262,144 here is FLOP per MXU per cycle. The units differ, so don't compare them directly.
Divide and it all fits: 262,144 FLOP ÷ 65,536 cells = 4 FLOP per cell per cycle, i.e. 2 MACs: one MAC = one multiply + one add = 2 FLOP, and two make 4.
That is the step §3.1 said “isn't in the figure”. Both sides multiply from MACs per cycle up to the published peak, so every number here stands.

⭐ How “592 small units” and “4 large ones” add up is §3.7's job; here, remember one pair: contraction dimension 16 vs. 256. Keep the two apart and §3.6's different tile sizes become obvious.
⚠️ A cross-generation warning Half of one TPU MXU's 131,072 MACs/cycle comes from “2 MACs per cell per cycle”, which only the 256×256 generations have; the older 128×128 ones (v3 / v4 / v5e / v5p) all do 1 per cell. Carry this constant across generations and you're off by 2×.
Three more plausible-sounding traps are folded below.
Where the wrong derivation fails, plus this model's three traps (reference · skip in class)
※ Common wrong derivation: two bad steps (moved from main text) ① It counts the wrong units. An SM has 4 Tensor Cores (one per sub-partition), not 1; CUDA cores number 128, not 4,096. The full chip has 592 Tensor Cores and 18,944 CUDA cores. 4,096 does exist, but as MACs per SM per cycle (4 Tensor Cores × 1,024), not a core count: familiar value, different units.
② It mistakes instruction shape for per-cycle throughput. mma.sync's m16n8k16 totals 16 × 8 × 16 = 2,048 MACs; one Tensor Core does 1,024 per cycle, so this instruction occupies it for 2 cycles. A package of work, not one cycle's. The largest, tcgen05.mma (128×256×16), is 524,288 MACs; at 4,096 per SM per cycle → 128 cycles; 64 with an SM pair.
⚠️ Three traps, each of which “sounds perfectly reasonable” ① That 16 is not the width of a GPU array; it is the instruction's contraction depth. A Tensor Core's 1,024 MACs/cycle is certain; their physical layout isn't public, so you can't square 16 into an “area”: that mixes two different units in one formula.
② Nor is 128 the square of 16 (that's 256). 128 = 131,072 ÷ 1,024 (MACs per cycle of one MXU vs. one Tensor Core); a ratio of MACs per cycle, unrelated to the array's side length.
③ The SM count is 148, not 128. They look alike, but one counts units, the other says how much bigger each unit is; their closeness makes the cancellation above work, but they differ.
⭐ The takeaway of this section One shape: a perfect fit on one side, half wasted on the other.
Neither design is worse; “whose granularity?” has two answers.

⭐ Back to fusion. Two numbers cap fusion size: stovetop size (§3.2b: 227 KiB vs. 64 MiB, 289×) and this granularity.
Small bench, fine grain: many small fusions. Big bench, coarse grain: one much larger fusion. §3.6 meets both at the tiling step.
⭐ Turning “289×” into “how big a tile can you actually use” Decisions hinge not on a ratio but on whether a tile fits. Same arithmetic, both sides: (head_dim = 128, bf16, K/V double-buffered, scores in fp32; real kernels keep Q and the accumulator in registers, so this is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a byte count.)
Br × Bc2×(K+V)QScoresTotal
64 × 6464 KiB16 KiB16 KiB96 KiB
128 × 6464 KiB32 KiB32 KiB128 KiB
128 × 128128 KiB32 KiB64 KiB224 KiB ← at the cap
256 × 256256 KiB64 KiB256 KiB576 KiB ← over cap
512 × 10241.0 MiB128 KiB2.0 MiB3.1 MiB

GPU thread-block cap, 227 KiB: 128 × 128's 224 KiB fits right at the ceiling; one step up is 2.5× the cap and overflows.
TPU core, 64 MiB: 2048 × 2048's 18.5 MiB fits with two-thirds to spare.

⭐ So “real FlashAttention kernels always use 64 or 128 block rows” isn't a tuning result; that 227 pins it down. Raise the cap to a few MiB and people would go bigger at once, as the TPU side does. ⚠️ §3.2b caveat: 64 MiB is the total; what one kernel may use at once is a separate budget. The last row fitting doesn't mean the compiler grants it all.

3.5 What each side added alone

So far: what one side has and the other lacks. Two pieces remain, one grown by each side.

The question isn't what they are, but: the product page says “supported”; can you use it?

Two examples, one per side.

GPU side: block-scaled quantization. The marketing line: “B200 supports FP4”.

True. But block-scaled instructions have two paths, on different dies; B200 has only one. (A warp-level instruction needs sm_120a: consumer dies only. tcgen05.mma's block_scale needs sm_100a: B200's only path. Figure: L300 G-5.)

⭐ Block scaling in hardware (NVFP4 vs. MXFP4, Blackwell's three additions, training-side 16×16): see Topic 8 · Precision and quantization.

TPU side: SparseCore, an embedding-lookup core. The marketing line: “the TPU has a core just for embedding lookups”.

Also true. But it pays off only when the same rows are looked up repeatedly. Recommenders, hammering a few hot rows, are its home turf.

Language models repeat too little (not zero). A 100K+-token sequence: only a few thousand distinct words, mostly the top 1–2K rows. Real repetition, but orders of magnitude below search/ads/recs, whose concentration sets SparseCore's break-even. This doesn't pay. The compiler never routes them there: zero table lookups in production.

⛔ “Can't use it” isn't “not using it”: you use this core daily Saying “language models can't use SparseCore” is wrong. What goes unused is only the table-lookup role.

Its real job in large-model training: offloading collectives, taking All-Gather and Reduce-Scatter off the TensorCore so it keeps computing while communication runs. One way the TPU overlaps compute and communication.

Sources are public: the Google Cloud blog “Training large models on Ironwood TPUs” lists it as its own tuning technique; the public MaxText repo's XLA flag library has SparseCore All Gather.

⭐ The deeper lesson: marketing doesn't just leave you unable to use what it advertises; it hides the part you already use. You search the profile for table lookups, find none, and conclude the core is idle.

So how does it handle irregular memory access? Take the core apart.

Now what it is: lift the lid.

In XLA, the “collectives” line is a set of flags. Here they are, so “offloading” is tangible, all from public sources:

flagTurns onKey point
① Main switches: collectives → SC
--xla_tpu_enable_sparse_core_collective_offload_all_gather All-Gather to SparseCore On Ironwood (v7) these three default to true.
So it already works for you, no flags set

…_offload_all_reduceAll-Reduce
…_offload_2d_all_gather All-Gather on a two-level mesh Must be enabled explicitly

--xla_tpu_use_tc_device_shape_on_sc SC reuses the TensorCore's device shape MaxText groups these four as ENABLE_SPARSECORE_OFFLOADING_BASE_FLAGS,
set to true / false / false / true. The trap: the main switch alone often does nothing

⚠️ Two constraints. First, Continuation Fusion and SparseCore offload are mutually exclusive; MaxText's comment: “Either one of CF or SC can be enabled at a time”. Both overlap comms with compute by routes that don't stack; “both on is faster” is the commonest misuse. Second, 98304 KiB = 96 MiB, larger than v7's 64 MiB of VMEM per core. The recipe uses it as a cross-generation limit request; the target machine caps the real value. Reported as is, without guessing why.

⛔ First: the two “Tensor Cores” are two orders of magnitude apart The easiest cross-platform spec-sheet mistake; it makes every “compute per core” figure wrong too.
NVIDIA Tensor CoreTPU TensorCore
What it isA unit inside an SM The device's main compute core
ContainsJust the matmul array MXU + VPU + scalar unit + VMEM
Per chip100+ SMs, each with several On v7: 2
⭐ So a TPU TensorCore corresponds not to a GPU Tensor Core but to the level of a whole GPU die. §3.7's “592 Tensor Cores vs. 4 MXUs” table rests on this; get it wrong and you read it backwards.
⭐ Second: scalar vs. vector is not weak vs. strong “1 scalar subcore per 16 vector” invites the misreading “scalar compute is weak, so only one”. Wrong.

• A vector unit does the same thing to a row of numbers: a thousand numbers, one instruction, all plus two.
• A scalar unit makes one decision: how many loop iterations? where is the next address? skip this batch?

⭐ Kind, not quantity: a decision has one answer; you can't make it a thousand times. So 1:16 is division of labor.
Not just SparseCore: TensorCore and GPU SM share the trio. It's the machine's skeleton. 0-D/1-D/2-D is right; the error is reading it as strength.
⭐ Third: turning on both optimizations doesn't stack them The table's worst trap is the mutual exclusion, not a flag. Continuation Fusion (comms chopped into compute gaps; the TensorCore alternates computing and moving) and SparseCore offload (whole job outsourced next door) share one goal: two implementations of one thing.
The compiler rewrites that instruction one way only; both on = two passes fighting over one op.

⭐ The rule: before asking “is both on faster?”, ask if they are two ways of doing one thing. If so, both on doesn't stack; the compiler picks one arbitrarily. How CF works and the “picks one” source: Further reading 1.
⭐ Fourth: what MMA means, and why the TPU lacks it MMA = Matrix Multiply-Accumulate: one instruction computes D = A×B + C.
Remember: multiply and add are fused; the accumulator is far wider than the inputs: FP8/FP4 in, FP32 accumulation, no spill or rounding. ⭐ This makes 4-bit inputs usable: not that four bits suffice, but that they only feed the multiply; accumulation never loses precision.

Does the TPU have MMA? Mathematically yes, formally no. The difference isn't whether a matrix instruction exists but who decides when it runs. GPU: a thread issues it at runtime, hardware schedules, a scoreboard tracks. TPU: each cycle's issue is fixed at compile time.
⭐ The GPU made matmul an instruction; the TPU, a pipeline. §3.2d again, other unit. Warp → warpgroup → thread; sources: Further reading 3

Further reading: three topics the lecture may skip

Each came from a class question. Safe to skip; each pins down an easily blurred point.

Further reading 1: CF, and why it excludes SparseCore offload
CF = Continuation Fusion. Its goal is exactly the same as SparseCore offload's: overlap collectives with compute. Only the mechanism differs.

How CF works: it cuts one All-Gather into small chunks slipped into neighboring compute: the TensorCore computes, moves a chunk, computes again, alternating on the same core. Unfinished work passes to the next fusion as state, relay-style. That hand-off gives “continuation” its name.

How SparseCore offload works: the whole transfer goes next door; the TensorCore keeps computing.

Why only one? The MaxText config docs settle it: “The implementation (such as BC-offload or continuation fusion) is chosen based on other flag values.” Chosen. They're alternative implementations of one collective; the compiler picks one to rewrite that instruction. Turn both on and two passes fight over one op.

⭐ The takeaway: before asking if two optimizations stack, ask if they're two ways to do one thing. If so, they don't; the compiler picks one. Sources: public MaxText repo, src/maxtext/configs/README.md and benchmarks/xla_flags_library.py. Continuation-state passing between async collective fusions: public tech blogs; neither NVIDIA nor Google has published a formal CF design doc.
Further reading 2: Scalar, vector, matrix units (I always mix them up)
The intuition is right: sort by dimension. Scalar: one number at a time (0-D); vector: a row (1-D); matrix: two 2-D tiles (2-D). Shape-wise, that's it.

⛔ The common mistake is to read them as tiers of compute, as if a scalar unit were a weak vector unit. They do different kinds of work.

· A vector unit does the same thing to a row of numbers. 1,000 numbers, one instruction: all +2.
· A scalar unit makes a decision. How many loops? Next address? Skip this batch?

⭐ The difference is kind, not amount: a decision has one answer; you can't make it a thousand times. “Weak” isn't a flaw: the job needs doing once.

An analogy: the vector core is a hundred line workers turning the same screw; the scalar core is the one holding the order: “this batch, line three.” One is enough.

Back to the figure: SparseCore has 1 scalar subcore to 16 vector subcores. That ratio is the division of labor, not a scalar-compute shortfall. Orange dashed (commands) leave the scalar subcore; blue solid (data) are the 16 tiles each fetching their own. The commander doesn't haul data.

⭐ The most useful point: this trio isn't specific to SparseCore. The TensorCore has the same three layers: scalar unit + vector unit (VPU) + matrix unit (MXU). So does a GPU SM. The whole machine is built on this skeleton, so you won't have to sort it out again elsewhere.
Further reading 3: What is MMA? On TPU too?
MMA = Matrix Multiply-Accumulate. One instruction computes D = A×B + C.

In hardware it is special in three ways, each saving real cost:
  • ① One instruction = a whole small matmul, not one scalar multiply-add. Fetch/decode spread over hundreds of MACs: saves scheduling.
  • ② Fused multiply-add, wider accumulator. FP8/FP4 in, FP32 accumulate, no write-out or rounding between. ⭐ 4-bit inputs work not for accuracy: they only feed multiplies; adds stay 32-bit.
  • ③ Operands are reused inside the unit. A scalar loop re-reads each element of A for every column of B; an MMA unit reads it once, reuses it across the tile: the source of arithmetic intensity (Section 1's line).
⭐ Across generations, the instruction keeps getting bigger and the issuer smaller.
GPU genIssued byOperands in
Volta – AmpereOne 32-thread warp, in sync Private registers, one fragment each
HopperOne 128-thread warpgroup, async A straight from shared memory
BlackwellOne thread, fire and forget Shared + Tensor Memory (incl. accumulator)

The Blackwell row's “issued by a single thread” is from Colfax Research's Blackwell Tensor Memory tutorial (“can and must be issued by a single thread”; the PTX ISA officially says “single thread semantics”). The reason: none of its data sits in private registers; it all lives in CTA-shared memory, so the matrix unit is decoupled from the warp scheduler.

So does the TPU have MMA? Mathematically yes, formally no: that gap is this lecture's thread.

The MXU multiply-accumulates too. The question isn't whether a matrix instruction exists, but who decides when it runs. GPU: threads issue an MMA at runtime; hardware schedules it, the scoreboard tracks it. TPU: the machine is VLIW; each cycle's issue is fixed at compile time: no scoreboard, no out-of-order, not even threads.

⭐ The GPU turned matmul into an instruction; the TPU, into a pipeline. An instruction is issued, scheduled and tracked; a pipeline runs on schedule as data flows through.
⚠️ A long-standing confusion: “Tensor Core” means things two orders of magnitude apart · NVIDIA's Tensor Core is an execution unit inside an SM. A B200 has over a hundred SMs, each with several.
· The TPU's TensorCore is the device's main compute core, holding the MXUs, VPU, scalar unit and VMEM. A v7 chip has only 2.

⭐ So the TPU TensorCore corresponds not to the GPU Tensor Core but to an entire GPU die. The easiest cross-platform spec-sheet mistake; it makes every “compute per core” figure wrong too.

⭐ The takeaway: Blackwell's moves (accumulator out of registers, single-thread issue, operands in dedicated memory) point to the TPU. For matmul, it deliberately dropped “a fragment per thread” dynamism for bigger tiles, less scheduling overhead. Elsewhere, the GPU stays the do-anything dynamic machine. The paths haven't merged, but on the money-maker, they're a step closer.

Sources: NVIDIA PTX ISA docs (three gens: mma / wgmma / tcgen05.mma), CUTLASS Blackwell feature docs, Colfax Research's Blackwell Tensor Memory tutorial. “Blackwell is moving toward the TPU” is my judgment, not official from either side.
⭐ First half: five layers, one kind of missing thing Chip → core → floor plan → parallel hierarchy → instruction. At every layer the TPU lacks something.
Never a compute unit. Always cache, scoreboard and “decide at runtime” machinery: all there because the hardware doesn't know what you'll run.

⭐ Section 0's claim, now checked five times: everything differs, and each difference traces to “it already knows what you'll run.”
The second half reassembles all five.
Section 3b

⭐ Rebuilt: FlashAttention, side by side

All the first half's parts now work at once.
Two jobs. First, walk one op end to end (§3.6). Then pay off two earlier claims: §3.6's end settles Section 0's “different everywhere, but only one cause”; §3.7 explains Section 1's coincidence: same-range peaks.

3.6 ⭐ Climax: one FlashAttention, side by side on both chips

Two questions: how much fits in one pan (on-chip memory)? What holds each side back?

The op picked in Section 2 now runs once on each chip.

🍳 A kitchen analogy; every later number hangs on it Picture a three-step dish: chop, stir-fry, plate.
The clumsy way: chopped food goes to cold storage, out to be fried, back, out to be plated. Three steps, four trips.
The catch: the half-done food is huge. Ingredients: 100+ MB. Intermediate: 30+ GB, 256× bigger. Four trips: 100+ GB on the road, not one cut made.

⭐ FlashAttention in one line: all three steps on the stovetop at once; the intermediate never leaves it.

Three mappings to keep:
• Cold storage = HBM (off-chip main memory: big but far)
• Stovetop = on-chip scratchpad (GPU shared memory, TPU VMEM: small but close)
• Blade width = how much one instruction bites (§3.4's 16 vs. 256)
Both opening questions live here: pan size = stovetop size; the limit = stovetop or blade.

Now real numbers. First: why is tiling unavoidable? Section 2's “demand exceeds supply 5×” was a ratio; here are absolute sizes.

This is §1–2's operator fusion (expand to compare)
⭐ This figure is the operator fusion from Sections 1 and 2, laid out end to end 🍳 In the analogy, fusion means “all three steps on the stovetop in one go.” Red, left: a cold-storage trip per step; green, right: all on the stovetop.
Unfused, the 32 GiB S lands in HBM between steps; fused into one kernel, the S term disappears.

⭐ Every fusion has this cost profile, not just FlashAttention: zero FLOPs saved; all savings in the “intermediates never land” row. Hence Section 1 made “compute ÷ bandwidth” the course's master ratio: fusion is the only technique moving you right on the roofline via the data path, not the math.

⚠️ The math is unchanged, so hardware, not the algorithm, sets the ceiling: how much fuses depends on what fits on-chip. The paths below differ in how far the same fusion goes per chip.

How does each side delete it? We walk each path alone, then side by side. On purpose: a table up front makes everything look different; walked separately, most stops match.

Now side by side: the main figure of the lecture.

⭐ In plain English Row ② (an extra automatic cache tier) was covered in §3.2–3.2c. Row ⑥ is new: who decides when to hand off. The dish hops between the matrix burner and the vector burner. The GPU picks on the fly, whoever is free; the TPU sets the roster in advance, to the minute. That's all of Section 5; just planted here.

⭐ Count with Section 1's test: of six stops, only these two exist on one side and not the other; the other four do the same job. Other differences exist, but they are only parameters such as capacity and naming (the largest is the 289× at stop ③), and they change next generation.
Fusion size is capped by two numbers together (from §3.4; expand)
⭐ From §3.4's close: two numbers jointly cap fusion size The first number, just drawn as area: stovetop size. A GPU thread block gets at most 227 KiB.
Three 128×128 bf16 tiles (Q/K/V) = 3 × 128 × 128 × 2 B = 96 KiB; add double buffering and you're near the limit.
On the GPU, tile size runs straight into capacity. The TPU's 64 MiB is 289× that; capacity isn't what holds it back.

The second: §3.4's granularity, how wide one instruction bites. Contraction dimension: GPU 16, TPU 256. head_dim=128 is exactly 8 × 16 on the GPU, every cut clean; on the TPU it fills only half the 256-wide edge.
How the two divide up, 🍳 in kitchen terms:
The GPU's stovetop is too small. You cook in small batches, refetching the same ingredients: K/V re-reads.
The TPU's stovetop is too big to fill; its knife is too wide. A 256-wide blade on 128-wide ingredients: half of it cuts air.
Same job, different walls. That's why §3.4 said to read the two numbers together; either alone misleads.
⭐ Same fusion, two chips: three differences seen only side by side ① Walls capping tile size: one on the GPU, three on the TPU.
GPU: only capacity, 227 KiB, so go as big as fits. Small tiles mean K/V reloads.
TPU: three. Upward, capacity (backward overflows first) and, sooner, parallelism (big tiles leave one KV block; the pipeline collapses: fits, but slower). Downward, per-tile overhead. So on the TPU, “bigger is better” is wrong.

② The GPU must decide who splits, who shares; the TPU never asks.
Hundreds of small GPU units share the work, so you pick a dimension to split; pick wrong and you need a reduction, sync and sum.
On the TPU, one core takes one head's Q tile start to finish. Parallelism: the VPU's 8×128, a core's MXUs, the chip's two cores; no “farm out to hundreds, then merge” step. (Which split avoids merging, and why the two FA versions swapped roles over it: Topic 3, Section 1.)

③ Identical MACs, different reachable peak.
Same math, same FLOPs. The GPU pays in data movement (K/V re-reads), the TPU in idle cycles.
The TPU idles on shape: head_dim = 128 meets a 256-wide MXU in both matmuls: as contraction dim in QKᵀ, output dim in PV. So MXU utilization caps at 50%, and no kernel parameter fixes it. That holds at the kernel-parameter level. The real ways out (§3.4): change head_dim (a model-architecture call, not tuning: 32 heads × 128 → 16 heads × 256 measured +21% / +32% / +46% MFU at 8K / 16K / 32K), or a fully transposed pipeline.

⭐ All three in one line: the array has two spatial dimensions and one temporal. Unfilled space idles; too little time can't amortize weight loads. head_dim = 128 falls in between: too small to fill space, too short to serve as time. The far smaller GPU array fits 128 any way: it hits capacity; 128 can't fill the TPU's: it hits shape. (Where this test comes from, and why all three dataflows fail it: the two folds in §3.4.)

⭐ The rest is FlashAttention's story: the inner/outer-loop figure, why versions swapped loops, measured tile sweeps, three-layer efficiency ceilings. All in Topic 3 · The evolution of attention, Section 3. Here it's just the vehicle.

The stovetop's second limit: delivery speed (analogy addendum)
🍳 The stovetop's second limit, after area: delivery speed The two walls govern “how much you can fuse”; Section 1's 64 governs whether fused is still fast. The trip from cold storage doesn't vanish; it moves to another road, with its own width. So after fusing, redo the math: compare the new intensity against 64, not 312.

Last figure. Ignore the stops; count what you must write, the coder's side.

⭐ Walk complete: Section 0's claim holds Four of six rows match. Evidence for “different everywhere, but only one cause”: no cherry-picked example, the whole path counted.
(The two differing rows are one question: auto-cache and hand-off scheduling both ask whether the decision waits for runtime.)
Section 2's 4 runtime decision points are now concrete: the left rows you type by hand.

⚠️ Don't read “shorter right column” as “TPU is less work.” One wrong character in those declarations and the compiler won't catch it. Left: “many decisions.” Right: “one chance to get it right.”

3.7 Section 1's coincidence: why the peaks are in the same range

Section 1 set the peaks side by side (2,307 vs. 2,500), same range, no why. Now we compute it. The first half's two most different numbers cancel.

🍳 The next figure, as one picture Nearly the same total blade, cut completely differently: many small knives versus a few big ones.

⭐ The question isn't “who has more compute” but “how many pieces, of what size”.

Watch the tally on the right. The knife has two sizes, both shown; don't merge them. Blade width (bite depth): §3.4's contraction dimension, 16 vs. 256. Cut per stroke (MACs/cycle): 1,024 vs. 131,072 (one Tensor Core vs. one MXU), 128× apart.

⭐ Remember the right-hand 148 ÷ 128 Not approximate, exact: 148 ÷ 128 = 1.156, and 606,208 ÷ 524,288 = 1.156.
“148× more units” and “128× smaller units” nearly cancel: the real reason the peaks are close. The TPU recovers the last 1.16× with clock: 2.2 vs. 1.83 GHz is 20% higher: at 1.83 GHz the B200 does 606,208 × 2 × 1.83 GHz ≈ 2,219, so 2,307 leads by about 1.04×; the figure's bottom-right 1.03× uses the official 2,250, which implies about 1.86 GHz (NVIDIA doesn't publish the exact clock).
⚠️ This chain is for the HGX-board B200. Section 1 used 2,307 vs. 2,500: the NVL72 GB200 clocks about 2.06 GHz, so the TPU leads by under 10%, too little to offset 1.16×; hence Section 1's “GPU 8% higher.” Unit count and size match in both comparisons, so the peaks always share a range; who leads depends on the chip you pick.

⭐ Every ratio in this lecture measures piece size, not compute. Same order of silicon on both: 592 small pieces versus 4 big ones.
Section 4

Wiring 64 chips: two different answers

This is background for Section 6's measurements.
Those are 64 vs. 64, and the two sides wire them in structurally different ways.
Hardware only: link count, width, shape, worst-case hops. Which patterns suffer, and why expert parallelism (EP) is most topology-sensitive, is about sharding: Topic 5.

In one line: NVL72 is a switched domain; ICI is a direct-connect network.
The domain is capped at 72 chips, but any pair inside is one hop, wherever they sit. The network has no switches and links only neighbors, but one protocol scales to 9,216 chips.
64 sits where they differ most: under NVL72's cap, all one hop; on ICI, a 4×4×4 torus, 6 hops at worst.

⚠️ Two easily confused 900s Hopper's 900 is bidirectional; Blackwell's 900 is unidirectional. Same number, different quantity.
Blackwell: 1,800 bidirectional, 900 unidirectional. A GB200 board has two B200s, so the superchip totals 3,600 GB/s; each GPU is still 1,800. The general trap: one number, two generations, two conventions; ask which generation, which direction.

But reach is not what you actually get. Below are our own numbers: not vendor specs but the measured drop.

⚠️ Know what these are: different evidence from the two figures above. Those show structure; these are one side's measurements: GPU only, 8 to 32 GPUs in one NVL72 domain, not a comparison. We never ran the TPU counterpart (no torus collective measured). One point: “no distance in the domain” does not mean “no cost in the domain.” Which pattern suffers on which topology is again Topic 5.

⛔ The likeliest misreading 9,216 ÷ 72 = 128 measures only topology reach, not who runs faster. Reading it as “TPU clusters are 128× faster” is the course's easiest mistake, and the hardest to catch yourself.

⭐ Carry this into Section 6: its two numbers ran on two structurally different networks: one hop in a domain vs. up to six. We never split “faster compute” from “better wiring.” ⚠️ And we never measured collectives on a torus, so: structure, not speed.
The four comm primitives, NVL72 internals, cross-chip addressing: L300 §4; which sharding suits which topology: Topic 5.
Section 5

⭐ Runtime vs. compile time, unpacked

You've met this pair four times: §2.1's “4 vs. 0”; §3.3's runtime-only layers; §3.3b's three circuit sets; §3.6's two forking stops (of six).
Each hit this decision on a different part. Now the decision itself: who schedules, and how that flows from hardware to your code.

5.1 Hardware: who owns latency

The bottom layer is clearest. A load takes hundreds of cycles; who fills them? It's about responsibility, not speed.

When each scheme fails The failure conditions matter, not the mechanism. The GPU fails when it runs out of stand-ins.
Register pressure leaves fewer warps resident (that count is occupancy), exposing latency. Hence tuning often starts by cutting registers.
The TPU fails when it can't predict.
Dynamic shapes or runtime-only addresses leave the compiled schedule idle.
One fears tight resources, the other uncertainty. Remember it and you can derive, not memorize, L300 §5.5's porting costs.

5.2 Code: same job, two ways

The difference shows up verbatim in code.

Collectives, one level up, follow suit. GPU: you hand-write all-reduce as the training loop's second step. TPU: you never write it; the compiler inserts it from your declared parallelism. (Code pair: L300 §5.3.)

5.3 The compiler's limits

Natural reaction: “Why not leave it all to the compiler?” You can't; the line is clear.

⭐ Where FlashAttention falls “Both sides hand-write it” completes §3.6's comparison table: the TPU spares you data movement, not algorithms. Full inference-engine porting costs, and what AOT can precompute: L300 §5.5 / §5.6.
⭐ Fusion, closed: two different things You may have tripped: the figure credits fusion to the compiler, yet the note says it can't do FlashAttention. Both hold: two kinds of fusion.

① Fusion that keeps the math: the compiler's job. Top-left cell: same math, no cold-storage trip. You write none; both compilers do it silently.
② Fusion that needs new math: always human.
FlashAttention fuses only because softmax was first rewritten to merge blockwise.
Plain softmax can't: its denominator sums the whole row, so nothing is output until the row is seen, nor can a small block stay on the stovetop. Online softmax fixes exactly that: running max and denominator update as it goes, one rescale at the end, identical results. The algorithm was swapped to enable fusion, not tweaked after. The compiler may decide how, not what, is computed.

⭐ “Who decides fusion?” Two halves:
• Whether and how much: the hardware (§3.6's stovetop and blade width jointly cap it)
• Who does it: whether the math changes (no: compiler; yes: you)
The paradox: fusion, the course's constant thread, is neither pure hardware nor pure software: on the seam, where all hardware study lands.

⚠️ Don't misread §3.6's “not a single FLOP is saved”: it counts the two matmuls. Online softmax's per-block rescale is O(n·d), negligible next to O(n²·d). “Keeping the math” means equivalent results, not zero extra instructions.

5.4 The objection: isn't CUDA Graph compile-time too?

Now the strongest objection, half right: record a whole step's graph once, run it straight through: the gains are real, often an order of magnitude.

What it overturns depends on why it's fast. The usual answer is wrong: it saves not “branches” but per-kernel launch CPU cost. So: which layer does it freeze?

What does CUDA Graph really produce, and who replays it? (four follow-ups)
① It doesn't produce code: not a single new line. Instantiation yields work descriptors: per node, which already compiled kernel entry to call, grid and block sizes, shared memory, where the parameters live, dependencies. The kernels are the same CUBINs as before, byte for byte. ⭐ NVIDIA named the API cudaGraphInstantiate: instantiate, not compile. Accurate.

② Operator fusion? None; not won't, can't. CUDA Graph can't see inside kernels: each node is an opaque entry address plus parameters. It doesn't know what you're computing.
⭐ It isn't on XLA's level at all: XLA works on HLO and sees the math, so it fuses ops, picks layouts, allocates buffers, schedules collectives, then emits new kernels; CUDA Graph emits nothing.
In one line: XLA, a compiler, changes what code runs; CUDA Graph, a submission list, changes only how it's submitted. The shared “graph” is chance.
📌 The two are complementary: XLA's GPU backend can wrap its kernels in a CUDA Graph to cut launch cost. Fuse first, then package.

③ Where does “replay” happen? ⚠️ First, a near-universal myth.
Kernel code lives on the GPU; a normal launch never uploads code. The CUBIN sits in device memory from module load; 10,000 launches don't move it.
Where do a launch's 5–10 µs go? The CPU builds a launch packet live: packing args, validating, writing the command buffer, ringing the doorbell. Small, but per kernel.
⭐ So CUDA Graph saves not “uploads” but the CPU rebuilding N launch packets every time. What moves to the GPU is launch metadata, not kernels.
⛔ Why it matters: if it saved uploads, bigger kernels would gain more; in fact smaller, more numerous ones do: it saves count, not size.

Two easily missed savings:
• Dependencies are enforced in hardware: NVIDIA: it “enforces the dependencies with hardware accelerations, instead of relying solely on CUDA streams and events.”
• The gap between nodes shrinks: purely device-side, not the CPU.

So who walks the nodes? The GPU. NVIDIA: the first launch “is responsible for uploading the work descriptions for a CUDA Graph to the GPU,” and a repeat launch means “launching a graph that has already been uploaded to the device.”
⭐ Stronger indirect evidence: replay's CPU cost barely depends on graph length (the NVIDIA post's title: “Constant Time Launch for Straight-Line CUDA Graphs”). If the CPU replayed node by node, cost would grow with node count. It's constant: the CPU isn't walking them.
📌 Since CUDA 12 a kernel can launch a graph: literal “replay inside the GPU”, but a different API and purpose; see below.

④ After replay, did the two lower layers change? Not at all. Each graph node is still a normal kernel launch, with a grid. The work distributor picks each block's SM at runtime, by free resources; the graph doesn't, and can't, record that. Same for clusters.
Inside the SM, same: which warp issues this cycle is still the scoreboard's call, hardware tracks operands, a load's hit is still luck (§3.2d: 30 vs. 659).

⭐⭐ Root cause: CUDA Graph works outside kernels; blind inside, it controls nothing there.
So the three-layer claim hardens: it doesn't just happen to freeze layer one; architecturally, it can't reach the other two. Submission can't rule execution.

📌 Appendix: host-side vs. device-side launch, which matters more? They solve different problems: host-side, “same work, many times” (volume); device-side, “next step depends on this step's result” (possibility), NVIDIA's positioning: dynamic control flow.
For today's large-model workloads, host-side dominates: steps are essentially static (shapes fixed ahead, routing padded to fixed capacity, precisely to keep the graph static). ⚠️ Inferred from design intent and common framework use; I have no measured comparison; measure to confirm. ③ quotes: NVIDIA Technical Blog, “Constant Time Launch for Straight-Line CUDA Graphs.”
⭐ Takeaway for §3–5: the objection is their best evidence Location settled, the point runs the other way:
① CUDA Graph itself needs static shapes: a new shape forces re-capture, the TPU's much-faulted static tax.
② The TPU doesn't need it: XLA already compiles the step as one program. CUDA Graph patches a problem of the GPU's own making.
③ Most important: hardware cost is set by the worst case it must support, not the case you run. Even with graphs on every workload, §3.2's five components stay: at tape-out nobody knew if you'd use them.

For this performance, the GPU must become more TPU-like, yet only the top layer can move earlier. If the others could, those transistors would be long gone.

5.4b Second objection: isn't TMA making data movement TPU-like?

It deserves more than CUDA Graph: it points the right way.

The trend down §3.3b's four generations:

  • Always: plain loads via registers; threads compute addresses, strides, bounds; math waits for the copy.
  • From Ampere: cp.async skips registers; threads still compute addresses.
  • From Hopper: TMA. One thread fills a descriptor, fires it, moves on; hardware handles strides, offsets, bounds. 32-lane address math: deliberately abandoned.
  • From Blackwell: tcgen05 goes furthest. One thread issues MMAs for the whole CTA; operands and accumulators live in a dedicated 256 KiB/SM matrix scratchpad; results never return to registers.

Four GPU generations on: whole blocks, by descriptor, no threads held, into a software-managed scratchpad. Exactly the day-one TPU.

⭐ Only halfway; the other half is our thread How data moves converged: granularity (whole blocks), address generation (dedicated hardware, not 32 lanes), operand destination (a scratchpad, not registers). All three really do.
Who decides hasn't moved at all:
• TMA descriptors are built at runtime, not compiled in; shapes may change, you rebuild.
• L1/L2 remain; hits still known only at runtime: three of §2.1's four decisions live on.
• The warp scheduler still picks live, every cycle.

So not “the GPU is becoming a TPU,” but “the GPU made feeding TPU-like; who gives orders hasn't moved.” The sides never differed on the endpoint, only on who issues the DMA.
⚠️ Not imitation: the same constraint The faster the matrix unit, the less feeding may tie up compute. When one MMA eats tens of KB in a few cycles, 32 threads taking turns at addresses and register hops gatekeep their own compute.
Same physics, same answer; one vendor took four generations, the other shipped at the endpoint. The course's thesis, in time: not cleverness, one decision pushed through.
Sections 6–7

Can the two numbers be compared?

§3.6's six stops are done, but the two numbers below aren't from them. FlashAttention was structure and theoretical bounds (§2.3's figure notes “real Flash re-reads K/V; intensity never reaches 65,536”); the only like-for-like measurement: one pair of full-model Hunyuan3-295B runs.
So they pay off Section 1's line, not §3.6's side-by-side. First how to read them, then the numbers.

6.1 First, how to compare

Both usual comparisons fail. Peaks: what the chip can do, not your job's speed. MFU: pick a denominator, pick a conclusion. Only the figure's tier ③ stands.

⚠️ Procurement wants the figure's ④ (per dollar / per watt), but no shortcut: ④'s numerator is ③. Without ③ measured, ④ is a ratio of two unknowns.

“Pick a denominator, pick a conclusion”: no scare tactic; we fell for it once (methodology)
⭐ “New denominator, new conclusion” is no scare tactic: we fell for it once Same run, same numerator 854.0, two MFUs reported:

• 854.0 ÷ 2,700 = 31.6% (committed 2026-08-05, stood for 26 days)
• 854.0 ÷ 2,500 = 34.16% (corrected 2026-08-31, the current figure)

A 2.6-point gap, no rerun; not one digit of the measurement changed.

⛔ What went wrong: that 2,700 was inferred, not looked up.
Its author took HGX B200's 2,250 × 1.2 = 2,700: “Ultra must be a bit faster.”
But NVIDIA has never published a 2,700. GB300 NVL72's dense BF16 peak equals GB200's.
Blackwell Ultra raises dense FP4 (1.5×) and attention (2×), not BF16.

⭐ The lesson isn't “be careful”; it's why it was hard to catch.
2,700 looks just like an official spec: right units, right magnitude, plausibly above GB200. Nothing throws an error. The downstream 31.6% hides better still: honestly computed, flawless arithmetic.
So “was this number derived?” asks about the number you cite, not you. One of our eight retractions; the full log (incl. which way each skewed) is in L300 Appendix A.

6.2 ⭐ The numerator: one run, two utilizations

That figure covered only the denominator. The numerator has two named flavors, both in use; unless you know which was reported, you can't compare.

One line: numerator = what the model's math needs, or what the hardware actually ran?

🍳 The knife again: cuts needed vs. cuts made Same denominator: the hardware's peak cuts per second.
MFU's numerator = cuts the recipe needs; HFU's = cuts you actually made (botched redos and air cuts included).
So HFU ≥ MFU always; the gap is wasted cuts.

Which to read depends on the question:
• “Is the knife idle?” → HFU
• “When is dinner ready, at what cost?” → MFU (wasted cuts won't speed dinner a second)

The figure's 4/3 is an upper bound (full-layer recompute). Where does ours land? FlashAttention's backward recomputes the forward S once, wasting 1 of 7 matmuls (2 forward + 4 backward + 1 recompute): 7 ÷ 6 ≈ 1.167×, 85.7% useful. Both 1.167 and 1.33 are derived by definition, not measured. Overheads (16.7% vs. 33%) differ 2×; “recompute enabled” alone says nothing.

⭐ Third, easiest to get wrong: the roofline's numerator For “will I hit the roof?” use the HFU-side numerator, with recompute and padding.
Recompute really occupies matrix-unit cycles; hardware can't tell wasted work.

⚠️ Plot useful FLOPs and the error is one-sided: always an underestimate. Useful ≤ executed, so you think the ridge is far, add recompute, and crash through.
Example: an op that is 30% recompute: 312.5 × 70% = 218.8. Useful intensity is just 219; with recompute it's already 312. You think there's ample memory-bound headroom; you're already over.

One run, two questions, two numerators: HFU's to judge your side, MFU's to report output. Also how to use Section 1's line; derivation in Section 2's final collapsible.
⚠️ Trap: before comparing hardware, ask “same recompute?” Recompute fully off on one side, on at the other: HFU close, MFU far apart, or vice versa. Both read as “utilization”; they measure different things.

This explains item ③ of §6.3's closing figure (“what this ratio still lacks”): the recompute policies differ entirely.

6.3 Both sides, measured

Ticket in hand: skip the big numbers; read the two red segments first.

Hardest step next: not overstating this number. What does 1.31× still lack? List yours, then check below.
⚠️ Units first: the figure's 1.29 is per-chip TFLOP/s (854.0 ÷ 662.3); from here on we use per-chip token/s, 1.31 (6,242 ÷ 4,770). The gap is exactly the figure's 1.5%.

⚠️ The real output isn't the ratio The four red and two green point opposite ways: the number could move either way, and we've measured neither. Responsible work lists the unmeasured instead of rounding off.
Take away four questions: Was this number derived? Binary or decimal? Per chip, per device, or per core? Physical or usable? They work for any hardware pair. (The closing figure repeats them.) Tuning from 457 to 662.3, and what my checks missed: L300 §7 / §8.
Section 9

What is each good at?

Now the opening's open question. One sentence answers it; the rest qualifies.

9.1 Takeaway

From package to measurements, both chips are now taken apart. The opening promised “different everywhere, one cause”; in §3.6, four of six rows matched. Now, the cause.

⭐ Keep one thing: operator fusion. The figure gives the principle; fusion is the course's one end-to-end example, and it walks all three layers:
Why fuse: the only way right of the ridge point without changing the math (§1 · §3.6)
How much: stovetop size + blade width; two hardware numbers jointly cap it (§3.2b · §3.4)
Who fuses: math-preserving, the compiler; math-changing, always people (§5.3)

Physics, hardware, control: each layer sets one limit. That's why studying hardware always lands on fusion.

That's the course. No buying verdict, but given “N× faster,” you'll know the four questions and where its denominator and numerator are. Recall §6.2's two utilizations: same denominator, all the gap in the numerator.
